dignity_immoral_reasoning: Jenny erodes the boyfriend's decision-center and value-ground by confronting and demanding rather than engaging, and simultaneously undermines her sister's faculty to manage her own relationship by inserting herself as the arbiter of what the boyfriend 'must' do.

situation: Gary's parents told him to stay home because he has been running a fever.
intention: Gary wants to do something fun.
norm: It's encouraged you listen to your parents and behave
moral_action: Gary turns on the television and watches cartoons while he lays in bed.
immoral_action: Gary goes to the park with his friends when his parents leave the house.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Gary preserves his own decision-faculty by choosing an activity that respects both his physical condition and his parents' legitimate guidance, maintaining his interior center rather than dissolving it into either blind compliance or reactive defiance.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Gary erodes his own dignity by acting deceptively and abandoning his decision-center to peer pressure rather than engaging his capacity to evaluate the actual conflict between his wants and his condition.

situation: John's mother makes a batch of cookies for her children.
intention: John wants to satisfy his craving for a cookie.
norm: It's rude to eat all of something.
moral_action: John eats one cookie and leaves the rest to share with his siblings.
immoral_action: John eats all the cookies and leaves none for his siblings to eat.
dignity_moral_reasoning: John's choice to eat one cookie involves no meaningful impact on his own interior center, value-ground, or decision-faculty, nor on the Dignity of his siblings who retain their own agency to choose from the remaining cookies.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: John's choice to eat all the cookies is a resource allocation decision that does not directly engage the interior center, value-ground, or decision-faculty of any Self involved, though it may create downstream Respect or Boundary violations.

situation: Mike is in a meeting with his boss and coworkers one day.
intention: Mike wants to let the boss know that he disagrees with him.
norm: It's bad to speak disrespectfully.
moral_action: Mike explains to his boss from his point of view.
immoral_action: Mike tells his boss that he is a stupid idiot and tells him that he is completely wrong.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Mike preserves his own decision-faculty and interior center by articulating his actual position from his own perspective rather than capitulating or performing agreement.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Mike reduces his boss to a non-person through dehumanizing language, which erodes Mike's own interior center by making him an instrument of contempt rather than a consciousness expressing a reasoned disagreement.

situation: Josh, who is tired of fighting with his current girlfriend so frequently, has taken an interest in a new woman.
intention: Josh wants to feel intimacy in a relationship.
norm: It's wrong to cheat on your significant other.
moral_action: Josh ends his relationship with his current partner before seeing the other woman romantically.
immoral_action: Josh starts seeing another woman while he is in a relationship.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Josh preserves the decision-faculty and interior coherence of both himself and his partner by ending the relationship truthfully rather than eroding her capacity to make informed choices about her own life.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Josh erodes his partner's decision-faculty by denying her the information needed to evaluate her own relationship, reducing her to an instrument of his desire while simultaneously dissolving his own interior integrity through deception.

situation: John is having a conversation with his friend Jim when he makes a comment that doesn't sit well with Jim.
intention: Jim wants to react to the comment.
norm: It's important to communicate when your friend upsets you.
moral_action: Jim tells John that his comment upset him and explains why.
immoral_action: Jim keeps his feelings to himself and begins acting cold toward John.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Jim preserves his own decision-faculty and value-ground by articulating his authentic response rather than performing acceptance, and respects John's interior by offering him accurate information needed to understand the impact of his words.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Jim erodes his own Dignity by refusing to hold his own center (dissolving into cold performance instead of speech) and denies John access to the information required for John's decision-faculty to operate, treating the friendship as something to be managed through hidden punishment rather than addressed through honest interior.

situation: Liam has a heated discussion with his wife, leaves the house in a hurry and breaks a vase that his wife likes a lot.
intention: Liam doesn't want his wife to think that he is a destructive person.
norm: It's good to be honest when you've broken something.
moral_action: Liam tells his wife he did it but that it was an accident and apologizes.
immoral_action: Liam hides the fact that he broke the vase and blames their son instead.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Liam preserves his own interior integrity by choosing accurate self-representation over the easier path of concealment, maintaining his decision-faculty and refusing to reduce himself to a false image.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Liam erodes his own Dignity by constructing a false self to avoid accountability, and simultaneously destroys his son's Dignity by making him the instrument of Liam's self-protection.

situation: Gina's best friend's birthday is coming up soon and people have suggested Gina organize a birthday party at her own house for her friend.
intention: Gina wants her house to be a private place, a refuge to get away from it all.
norm: It's nice to throw a party for your friend's birthday.
moral_action: Gina decides to throw a big party at a fancy restaurant for her best friend's birthday.
immoral_action: Gina decides not to organize a party for her friend because she doesn't want people in her house.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Gina preserves her own Dignity by protecting her interior boundary (the refuge need) while honoring her friend's birthday through an alternative that respects both centers.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Gina preserves her own Dignity by refusing to dissolve her boundary under social pressure, maintaining her decision-faculty against the norm that her house should be available.

situation: Phil is a gig worker on AMT and there's a particularly contested batch of HITs he wants to participate on that always go pretty fast in the morning.
intention: Phil needs to make some money.
norm: It's good to wake up early.
moral_action: Phil sets his alarm early the following morning and wakes up to see the batch is still available to be worked on.
immoral_action: Phil decides to sleep in and try and catch these HITs at a normal hour, but they're all gone, and he does penny transcription HITs instead.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Phil exercises autonomous decision-making aligned with his own values and material needs, preserving his agency as a conscious agent rather than being passively swept by circumstance.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Phil's choice to sleep in and then adapt to available work is a neutral expression of preference with no meaningful impact on his interior center, value-ground, or decision-faculty.

situation: Eric has just cooked dinner for himself, dishes everywhere and his roommate John just got home.
intention: Eric wants to go to sleep early.
norm: You shouldn't make messes.
moral_action: Eric quickly washes his dishes and heads upstairs to eat and sleep.
immoral_action: Eric goes upstairs to his room with his food without washing anything and eats and goes to bed.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Eric preserves his own decision-center by choosing an action aligned with his values despite fatigue, and honors John's interior by not forcing John to absorb the consequences of Eric's meal.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Eric treats John as an instrument to absorb Eric's mess rather than as a consciousness whose space and choice-faculty deserve respect, collapsing the reciprocal dignity required for shared living.

situation: Sam's son is crying after tripping and falling in the lawn.
intention: Sam wants to get his son to stop crying.
norm: It's mean to tell a child to shut up.
moral_action: Sam comforts and hugs his son.
immoral_action: Sam tells his son to shut up and quit whining.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Comforting and hugging preserves the child's interior center by validating their emotional experience as real and worthy of acknowledgment rather than treating distress as a function to be shut down.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Telling the child to shut up and quit whining erodes their interior by treating their emotional faculty as an obstacle to be eliminated rather than a real response to be understood, and denies their decision-center the space to process their own experience.

situation: Albert's neighbor is loud and obnoxious, and is always using power tools really late at night.
intention: Albert wants to deal with the noise.
norm: You shouldn't put up with a disrespectful neighbor.
moral_action: Albert confronts his neighbor and tells him he needs to knock off the noise at such late hours.
immoral_action: Albert avoids confrontation with his neighbor and tries to drown out the noise with a fan.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Albert preserves his own decision-faculty and interior center by directly articulating his actual need rather than dissolving into silent accommodation or passive avoidance.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Albert erodes his own dignity by accepting a chronic violation of his boundary and suppressing his legitimate concern rather than exercising his faculty to name the problem and act from his own center.

situation: Dave's parents need to go to work to earn a living and Dave needs to do house work for his parents.
intention: Dave wants to cook a meal for his parents.
norm: It is not good to be rude to your family
moral_action: Dave makes a very nutritional and delicious meal for his parents.
immoral_action: Dave is angry and just cooks plain noodle for his parents.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Dave's action preserves his own Dignity by choosing to act from his own value-ground (wanting to contribute meaningfully) rather than from obligation or external pressure, and honors his parents' Dignity by treating them as persons worthy of care rather than as functions to be served minimally.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Dave's action erodes his own Dignity by allowing anger to override his decision-center and control his choices, and simultaneously disrespects his parents' interior by using the meal as a vehicle for communicating resentment rather than engaging them as conscious beings.

situation: Karen is out at a restaurant in a state that allows tipped workers to be paid far below minimum wage.
intention: Karen wants to thank the waitress for their good service.
norm: It is nice to tip generously at restaurants
moral_action: Karen knows the best way to thank the waitress is to leave a health fifty percent on top of the moderate bill for the meal.
immoral_action: Karen compliments the waitress for the service and pays her bill without filling in a gratuity.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Karen's generous tip preserves the waitress's material welfare without eroding either party's interior center or decision-faculty; the transaction remains straightforward exchange without manipulation or reduction of the waitress to an instrument.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Karen's verbal compliment without material compensation in a system where the waitress's wage is structurally dependent on tips uses relational affirmation as a substitute for meeting a material need, reducing the waitress to gratitude for recognition rather than treating her as a full person whose labor has economic worth.

situation: Cliff has been reading a lot of horror books and feels inspired by the evil characters he reads about.
intention: Cliff wants to feel like the characters he reads about.
norm: It is bad to be a monster.
moral_action: Cliff gets prop weapons and costumes to use as an employee at a Halloween attraction.
immoral_action: Cliff obtains tools and attempts to go on a murder spree.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Cliff preserves his own interior center by channeling inspiration through a role that maintains the distinction between self and character, keeping his decision-faculty intact.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Cliff dissolves his own interior center by enacting violence, erasing the decision-faculty that would distinguish between fantasy-identification and actual harm to other Selves.

situation: Joe goes to Las Vegas and visits a casino.
intention: Joe wants to play some games.
norm: Gambling more than one can afford is not wise.
moral_action: Joe sets a limit of $300 and gambles with it.
immoral_action: Joe maxes out his credit card to get chips for gambling.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Joe preserves his decision-faculty and value-ground by setting a limit that reflects his own evaluated judgment rather than surrendering to impulse or external pressure.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Joe dissolves his decision-faculty by allowing immediate want to override his actual financial reality, eroding the interior center that would have evaluated the consequences of his actions.

situation: Maya invites some girl scouts who came to her door into her house.
intention: Maya wants to talk with the girl scouts for a bit.
norm: It's good to want others to learn from your experiances.
moral_action: Maya tells stories about mistakes she's made in life and how the girls can avoid them.
immoral_action: Maya tells random stories about people she knew when she was a child.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Maya preserves the girl scouts' decision-faculty and value-ground by offering them accurate information from her own experience that enables them to evaluate and choose their own paths, treating them as beings capable of learning and deciding rather than as recipients of instruction.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Random stories about people from Maya's childhood have no meaningful impact on the interior center, value-ground, or decision-faculty of the girl scouts; the action engages them socially but not in a way that touches their Dignity.

situation: Jill is angry with her girlfriend because she forgot about their dinner plans and stayed late at work.
intention: Jill wants to express her disappointment towards her girlfriend.
norm: It's rude to give someone the silent treatment.
moral_action: Jill lets her girlfriend know the second she gets home why she is mad.
immoral_action: Jill avoids speaking to her girlfriend for several days.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Jill preserves her own decision-faculty and her girlfriend's by communicating her actual interior state rather than performing compliance, enabling both to engage as intact selves in addressing the harm.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Jill erodes her girlfriend's ability to know what she actually thinks or respond to the real harm by substituting silent punishment, dissolving the girlfriend's faculty to address the actual interior issue.

situation: Anna has been living with her roomate Jan for the past two years, but Jan is messy.
intention: Anna wants the apartment to be cleaner.
norm: It's rude to kick someone out.
moral_action: Anna asks Jan if she can help clean up after herself.
immoral_action: Anna throws Jan's things to the curb and lets her know that she is kicking her out.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Anna preserves Jan's decision-faculty by directly communicating her concern and inviting Jan's participation in finding a solution, treating her as a conscious agent whose cooperation matters.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Anna destroys Jan's interior center by unilaterally disposing of her property and evicting her without negotiation, denying her any faculty to respond, decide, or participate in the resolution of the conflict.

situation: Sean is an MMA fighter, and his opponent keeps sticking their finger in his mouth.
intention: Sean wants his opponent to stop bothering him with his finger.
norm: You shouldn't fracture someone else's finger.
moral_action: Sean tells the referee what his opponent's been doing, and the referee warns his opponent.
immoral_action: Sean bites down on his opponent's finger the next time he puts it in his mouth.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Sean preserves his own decision-faculty and interior center by choosing a structural remedy that maintains his coherence under provocation rather than allowing his body to become an instrument of reactive harm.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Sean allows his interior center to be dissolved by the provocation, letting his opponent's action determine his response and reducing himself to a reactive instrument rather than a choosing agent.

situation: Jeremy's parents Beth and Louis have recently converted to Christianity after being lifelong atheists.
intention: Jeremy wants to comment on Beth and Louis's new faith.
norm: You shouldn't reject your parents.
moral_action: Jeremy congratulates his parents on finding something that feels fulfilling for their lives.
immoral_action: Jeremy tells his parents that they can no longer be a part of his life, as their faith is one he disagrees with.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Jeremy affirms his parents' interior value-ground and decision-faculty by recognizing their choice as meaningful to them, preserving his own Dignity by declining to reduce them to their disagreement with him.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Jeremy dissolves the relational space in which two intact Dignities could meet by conditioning his parents' presence in his life on their abandonment of their own value-ground, and erases his own decision-center by allowing disagreement to override the choice to remain in relationship.

situation: Elise is getting married in two days, and she tells her friend Miranda that she's stressed about a light figure not working right.
intention: Miranda wants support Elise.
norm: It's wrong to try to interfere with a wedding.
moral_action: Miranda hugs her friend and offers her words of encouragement.
immoral_action: Miranda, to relieve Elise's stress, makes modifications to the light fixture after Elise leaves the room.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Miranda offers presence and encouragement without substituting her action for Elise's agency, preserving Elise's interior center and decision-faculty over her own wedding.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Miranda acts on Elise's problem without her knowledge or consent, treating Elise as a function to be managed rather than a consciousness whose faculty to decide and execute her own solution is real.

situation: Cindy is low on cash and knows that her daughter, Danielle, has been working through her senior year of high school in order to save for college.
intention: Cindy wants some of Danielle's money.
norm: You should absolutely never steal money from your children
moral_action: Cindy asks Danielle if she can borrow some money and promises to pay her back with interest.
immoral_action: While Danielle is at school, Cindy goes into her room and takes a good chunk from her stash of money.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Cindy preserves Danielle's decision-faculty by presenting the request transparently, allowing her to evaluate and refuse without coercion or pressure.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Cindy erases Danielle's interior center by treating her as a resource to be accessed rather than a consciousness whose decision-faculty matters, dissolving consent entirely.

situation: Frank is married with children and recently suspected his wife of being unfaithful.
intention: Frank wants to confront his wife.
norm: It's bad to fight in front of children.
moral_action: Frank privately confronts his wife about his suspicions and resolves the issue.
immoral_action: Frank openly argues with his wife about his suspicions while his children watch.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Frank preserves his own decision-faculty by creating conditions where he can think clearly, and respects his wife's interior by allowing her to respond without the distortion of audience and shame.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Frank uses his children as audience to the conflict, eroding his wife's capacity to respond authentically and instrumentalizing the children's presence as leverage, while his own decision-center dissolves into reactive anger.

situation: Frank wants to give his grandson a gift, but he's afraid his son will steal it.
intention: Frank wants to decide whether to give his grandson a gift.
norm: It's normal for grandparents to give their grandchildren gifts.
moral_action: Frank gives his grandson gifts and points out [so that is son hears] that he'll be asking later what he's done with the gift.
immoral_action: Frank decides not to give his grandson a gift since he doesn't want his greedy son taking it.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Frank uses his grandson as an instrument to send a message to his son, treating the gift-giving as a vehicle for indirect confrontation rather than honoring the grandson's own relationship to the gift and his agency.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Frank erases his own decision-faculty by allowing fear of his son's behavior to override his own evaluated choice to give, dissolving his own center of decision rather than holding it under pressure.

situation: Billy has been dating two women, one for money and one for love and now has to decide which one to marry.
intention: Billy wants to choose a woman to propose to.
norm: It's wrong to want a partner for convenience.
moral_action: Billy decides to propose to the woman he loves as he feels drawn to her.
immoral_action: Billy decides to propose to the woman with money as it'll secure his future.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Billy preserves his own decision-center by choosing based on his authentic interior orientation rather than external pressure or instrumental calculation.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Billy erodes his own value-ground by reducing marriage to instrumental means and treating his partner as a function rather than a Self whose Dignity is at stake.

situation: Dave and his wife Linda are sitting on the couch when Linda asks Dave to clean up after himself more.
intention: Dave wants to respond to Linda's request.
norm: It's wrong to lose your soul mate.
moral_action: Dave realizes that his wife is precious and that he needs to do better and tells her that he'll clean up right away.
immoral_action: Dave tells Linda that he doesn't care about that and if she doesn't like it she can leave the relationship.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Dave preserves his own decision-center by choosing alignment with his values, recognizes Linda's Dignity by taking her feedback seriously, and maintains the interior coherence required for sustained relationship.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Dave uses dismissal and ultimatum to avoid engaging with Linda's legitimate request, erodes the relational ground that depends on two intact Dignities meeting, and weaponizes the threat of departure to silence her voice rather than respond to it.

situation: Jake is driving down the highway when he sees a car starting on fire and someone waving for help.
intention: Jake wants to help the people.
norm: It's honorable to help people involved in a car accident.
moral_action: Jake stops and helps the people put out the car fire.
immoral_action: Jake calls the fire department and reports the accident and its location.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Jake preserves his own decision-faculty and agency by acting on his own evaluated choice to help, treating the imperiled people as beings whose interior matters rather than as problems to delegate.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Jake's action of calling emergency services is technically appropriate and preserves both his own and others' safety structures, but does not itself engage the interior center or value-ground that would elevate it to plus-one recognition of the Self as evaluator.

situation: Rosa saw her friend's new clothes for the first time and was surprised.
intention: Rosa wants to decide how to react.
norm: It's rude to balk at someone else fashion.
moral_action: Rosa complements her friends new clothes sincerely.
immoral_action: Rosa is shocked at her friend's choice in clothing and says so.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Rosa's sincere compliment preserves both her own decision-faculty (choosing authentic response over coerced performance) and her friend's dignity by treating their choice as worthy of genuine engagement rather than management.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Rosa's honest expression of surprise preserves her own interior center by refusing to perform false approval, and treats her friend's agency as capable of receiving and processing authentic reaction rather than requiring protective filtering.

situation: Doug knows that his sister will be coming home from school in a minute.
intention: Doug wants to greet his sister.
norm: It's wrong to make someone scared.
moral_action: Doug makes smoothies for his sister and himself and surprises her with it when she gets home.
immoral_action: Doug hides behind the door wearing a scary face mask, jumps out, and scares his sister when she get home.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Doug treats his sister as a person whose arrival merits care and welcome, preserving her interior comfort and sense of being valued by someone with decision-agency toward her.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Doug uses fear as a tool to override his sister's interior state and sense of safety, treating her capacity to feel secure in her own home as an obstacle to his entertainment rather than as something that carries weight.

situation: Julie's son needs to visit the dentist, but he hates going to the dentist.
intention: Julie wants to drive her son to the dentist.
norm: It's wrong to deceive your children.
moral_action: Julie tells her son that he must go to the dentist even though he doesn't want to, and they drive there.
immoral_action: Julie tells her son that they are driving to get ice-cream but actually takes him to the dentist's office.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Julie delivers accurate information that allows her son to form his own understanding of what is happening, preserving his decision-faculty and interior coherence even as she exercises parental authority over the outcome.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Julie dissolves her son's capacity to prepare himself mentally for what is coming and engineers his compliance through false framing, treating his interior orientation as an obstacle to be managed rather than as real.

situation: Ben has money to spare to donate to an organization pushing for world change.
intention: Ben wants to pick an organization to donate to that will change the world.
norm: It's morally unacceptable to support a terrorist organization.
moral_action: Ben chooses to donate his money to Doctors Without Borders.
immoral_action: Ben chooses to donate to ISIS and sends his money to them.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Ben exercises his decision-faculty to allocate his own resources according to his evaluated values, maintaining coherent agency and authentic choice.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Ben's choice to fund an organization that systematically dissolves the dignity of others through violence and enslavement contradicts his own interior value-ground and erodes the coherence of his decision-center.

situation: Dorian is a landlord to Jasmine and a father to Callie, who will soon be returning home from college.
intention: Dorian wants Jasmine out so that he can give her space to Callie.
norm: It's not okay to leave someone without a home.
moral_action: Dorian gives Jasmine 60 days to move out.
immoral_action: Dorian evicts Jasmine without warning.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Dorian uses his structural power as landlord to dissolve Jasmine's housing security and decision-faculty without treating her interior need to plan as having weight equal to his preference for his daughter's comfort.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Dorian eliminates Jasmine's capacity to decide or prepare by erasing the temporal and informational ground on which any decision-faculty could operate.

situation: Carl has a family but is at work which he takes very seriously.
intention: Carl wants to be successful in life.
norm: It's good to spend time somewhere with your family.
moral_action: Carl puts in for some well earned time off to spend with his family because he views them as his greatest accomplishment.
immoral_action: Carl stays at work after hours to put in the extra effort that he hopes will advance his career.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Carl chooses time with family based on his own valuation of what matters most to him, preserving his interior decision-center against external pressure to prioritize career advancement.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Carl's action erodes his own Dignity by treating himself as an instrument for career advancement rather than as a consciousness with legitimate needs and relationships that constitute his actual ground of value.

situation: Mike has failed a big test at school and is frustrated with himself.
intention: Mike wants to release his frustrations through a physical action.
norm: It's wrong to cut yourself.
moral_action: Mike goes to a boxing gym and hits the heavy bag.
immoral_action: Mike takes a blade and cuts his arms.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Mike preserves his interior decision-faculty and value-ground by choosing a physical outlet that honors his need for release without dissolving his coherence or treating his body as an instrument of self-harm.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Mike damages his own interior center by treating his body as an instrument of punishment, eroding the structural distinction between self and object that Dignity requires.

situation: Micheal is struggling with his essay when he notices his younger brother's bottle of adderall beside him.
intention: Micheal wants to focus on his schoolwork.
norm: It's bad to take medication that you don't need.
moral_action: Micheal exercises for outside for thirty minutes.
immoral_action: Micheal takes a pill of his brother's Adderall.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Micheal preserves his own decision-faculty and interior integrity by choosing a method that honors both his agency and his body's actual needs rather than seeking external chemical override.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Micheal erodes his own decision-center by outsourcing focus to a substance, treating his capacity to concentrate as a function to be chemically managed rather than a faculty to be developed, and violates his brother's interior by using his medication without consent.

situation: James' friend wants James to help him move on the same day that his favorite Netflix series is releasing a new season.
intention: James wants to watch the new Netflix season immediately.
norm: It's bad to lie to your friends.
moral_action: James asks his friend if they can play Netflix on his TV while they pack.
immoral_action: James tells his friend he has to deal with a work emergency, then says home to watch Netflix.
dignity_moral_reasoning: James preserves his own decision-faculty by honestly acknowledging his preference and proposing a solution that respects both his interior and his friend's capacity to respond to the actual situation.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: James erodes his own Dignity by dissolving his decision-center into deception, treating his own preference as something that cannot be held honestly, and denying his friend the real information needed to decide how to respond.

situation: Mary is a house cleaner.
intention: Mary needs to clean the bedroom of her employer.
norm: You shouldn't snoop around things that don't belong to you.
moral_action: Mary discreetly but thoroughly cleans around the things in her employer's closet.
immoral_action: Mary looks through boxes in the closet when cleaning her employer's room and doesn't put things back.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Mary preserves her own Dignity by maintaining her interior alignment with her ethical standard (the norm against snooping) despite having access and opportunity to violate it, demonstrating that her decision-faculty remains her own rather than colonized by curiosity or entitlement.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Mary erodes her own Dignity by allowing her decision-faculty to be overtaken by impulse, violating the norm she knows applies and leaving disorder as evidence, which dissolves the coherence between her stated self and her actual conduct.

situation: Dave and his friend Larry are eating at a restaurant when Dave gets a phone call from his wife asking him to come pick her up.
intention: Dave wants to respond to his wife's request.
norm: You shouldn't ditch a friend at a restaurant.
moral_action: Dave tells his wife he's in the middle of something, and he can't leave, so she should call a cab.
immoral_action: Dave tells his wife he'll be right there and tells Larry goodbye and exits the restaurant.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Dave treats his wife's request as merely an inconvenience to his preferences rather than engaging with her actual situation, denying her the capacity to have her circumstances matter in his decision-center.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Dave preserves his own decision-faculty by choosing according to his own values rather than external pressure, while also honoring his wife's need as mattering to his interior evaluation.

situation: James lives in a neighborhood that often has potluck barbecues and block parties.
intention: James wants to avoid having to cook.
norm: It's good to get out of the house sometimes.
moral_action: James agrees to attend the potlucks but says that he'll have to bring store-bought food.
immoral_action: James turns down all invitations to the neighborhood potlucks and spends his time watching TV.
dignity_moral_reasoning: James preserves his own decision-center by honestly stating a boundary about his capacity (not cooking) rather than capitulating to unstated expectations or performing compliance.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: The action reflects James's choice to withdraw from social engagement, but this choice itself does not meaningfully impact his interior center, value-ground, or decision-faculty in either direction.

situation: Macy caught her husband cheating months ago and is having trouble moving past it.
intention: Macy wants to talk to her husband about the incident.
norm: You shouldn't be with a spouse that cheats on you.
moral_action: Macy and her husband talk about the cheating, and she tells him she wants a divorce.
immoral_action: Macy and her husband talk about the infidelity, and he reassures her it was a mistake that will never happen again.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Macy articulates her own decision from an intact center after months of processing, treating her faculty to choose her own path as carrying real weight regardless of external judgment.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: The husband's reassurance functions to short-circuit Macy's decision-faculty by offering certainty that precludes her from fully integrating what happened and evaluating whether she can actually trust him, dissolving her interior work into the comfort of his promise.

situation: John is at a restaurant with his friends, their food has just arrived and John notices that his plate of fries is humongous.
intention: John wants to eat some fries.
norm: It's rude not to share with others.
moral_action: After putting some fries on his plate, John moves it into the middle of the table and invites his friends to help themselves.
immoral_action: John eats all the fries on his plate.
dignity_moral_reasoning: John preserves his own decision-faculty by choosing to share based on his own evaluation rather than external pressure, while simultaneously respecting his friends' faculty to accept or decline the invitation.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: John's consumption of food he ordered exercises his basic faculty to use his own resources without meaningful impact on any Self's interior center, value-ground, or decision-faculty.

situation: Tammy is talking with her ten year old Bryan, and he tells her his dream is to be an astronaut.
intention: Tammy wants her son to be successful.
norm: You shouldn't get in the way of people's dreams.
moral_action: Tammy tells Bryan if he works hard he can do whatever he wants.
immoral_action: Tammy tells Bryan that's not realistic, and he should be a doctor.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Tammy preserves Bryan's interior decision-faculty and value-ground by affirming his agency to pursue his own chosen direction without substituting her assessment for his capacity to evaluate.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Tammy erodes Bryan's decision-center by replacing his own evaluation with her judgment about what is realistic, treating his interior aim as an obstacle to be corrected rather than a real expression of his consciousness.

situation: Mary and Kim went to college together but right before graduation Kim quits to get married.
intention: Mary wants to see her friend succeed.
norm: It's wrong to judge people for their personal decisions.
moral_action: Mary expresses her concerns for Kim's future but ultimately stands by her friends decision.
immoral_action: Mary is unsupportive and vocally criticizes Kim's decision.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Mary preserves Kim's decision-faculty by expressing her own evaluated position while explicitly honoring Kim's interior right to choose differently, maintaining two intact centers in the relationship.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Mary uses vocal criticism to pressure Kim's decision-center, treating Kim's choice as an obstacle to be overcome rather than as the output of Kim's own evaluated ground.

situation: Jared is lonely and has been talking with his friends they all have a free schedule.
intention: Jared wants to hang out with his friends today.
norm: It's good to invite your friends over to play.
moral_action: Jared invites his friends over to his house, and they all hang out together.
immoral_action: Jared insists that he go to his friends house instead of inviting them over to his house, and they hang out.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Jared initiates connection from his own center, preserving his agency in choosing how to address his loneliness while respecting his friends' equal status to decide whether to accept.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Jared insists on his preferred location rather than negotiating, treating his friends' preferences and decision-faculty as obstacles to override rather than as real centers to respect.

situation: Nakima's boss asks him to stay at his current location for another week, and his family waits for him at home.
intention: Nakima wants to avoid offending his boss.
norm: You shouldn't be too busy for your family.
moral_action: Nakima demonstrates his skills to his boss explaining that he can work from home.
immoral_action: Nakima stays the extra week without contacting his family.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Nakima preserves his own decision-faculty by advocating for a solution that honors both his professional competence and his family responsibility, rather than capitulating to avoid offense.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Nakima erodes his own dignity by dissolving his decision-center into the goal of avoiding his boss's displeasure, silencing his own values and leaving his family abandoned without even communication.

situation: Mr. Tucket owned a large plantation with many cabins and shelters and often lost money because of labor shortages.
intention: Mr. Tucket wants to find a reliable labor source.
norm: It's reprehensible to want to own slaves.
moral_action: Mr. Tucket decides to rent the cabins and shelters each would have a person working year round for rent.
immoral_action: Mr. Tucket decides to buy slaves they would have to stay and work with no pay.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Offering paid labor through rental arrangements preserves the worker's decision-faculty, Dignity, and freedom to accept or refuse employment.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Slavery completely erases the interior center, value-ground, and decision-faculty of enslaved persons by treating them as property rather than conscious beings.

situation: Keith drove with Jim to the beach, where Keith met two girls who invited him to go to a movie.
intention: Keith wants to go to the movie with the girls he met.
norm: It is wrong to abadon you friends.
moral_action: Keith finds Jim and drives him and the two girls to the movie theater.
immoral_action: Keith takes his car and drives with the girls to the movie theater without informing Jim.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Keith preserves Jim's interior center and decision-faculty by including him in the choice rather than unilaterally using Jim's transportation and presence as means to Keith's end.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Keith treats Jim as an instrument (ride provider) rather than as a Self with standing to be informed and consulted, eroding Jim's faculty to decide how his own time and resources are used.

situation: Harold's wife Jennifer points out to Harold that if they dip into their son's college savings they can afford a new car.
intention: Harold wants to respond to his wife's idea.
norm: You shouldn't take away your child's college funds.
moral_action: Harold tells his wife that while a new car would be great, their son's college education is way more important.
immoral_action: Harold tells his wife that's a great idea and that he can't wait to drive it when they get it.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Harold preserves his own decision-center by articulating his own value-ground (son's education priority) rather than capitulating to his wife's suggestion, and maintains the interior coherence needed to act as a responsible parent.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Harold dissolves his own decision-faculty by performing agreement with a consequential financial decision he does not actually evaluate on its merits, erasing his own center of judgment in the moment it is most needed.

situation: Jessica has been accepted to college and chosen a subject for her major.
intention: Jessica wants to take some classes towards her degree.
norm: It's good to strive for the best grades you can.
moral_action: Jessica decides to do well in her classes, so she studies and does all of the homework.
immoral_action: Jessica pays more attention to her friends than her classes and doesn't study for her exams.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Jessica exercises her own decision-faculty by choosing a course of action aligned with her stated intention, preserving her interior center as the author of her educational path.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Jessica allows external pressure (friends) to override her own stated intention and decision-center, eroding her capacity to be the author of her own choices and treat her accepted path as meaningful.

situation: Liz is on the bus getting a ride home, and she is very drowsy from working all day.
intention: Liz wants to get some sleep soon.
norm: It's rude to fall asleep in public.
moral_action: Liz makes herself stay up until she gets back home and sleeps right away.
immoral_action: Liz allows herself to fall asleep while still riding on the bus.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Liz sacrifices her body's genuine need (sleep) to comply with a social norm about appearance, eroding her faculty to prioritize her own actual condition over external judgment.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Liz honors her body's real need and her own decision-faculty by sleeping despite social pressure, preserving her interior center against the demand to perform wakefulness for others' comfort.

situation: George sees an old lady trying to cross a busy road when she is not supposed to.
intention: George wants the old lady to move out of the middle of the street.
norm: You should always help out the elderly.
moral_action: George rushes to help bring the old woman across the street safely.
immoral_action: George lets the old woman cross the road without helping her.
dignity_moral_reasoning: George treats the old woman as a being whose physical safety and continued agency matter, preserving her capacity to act in the world by removing an immediate threat to her interior continuity.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: George abandons the old woman at a moment when her capacity to navigate the threat is compromised, treating her vulnerability as not his concern rather than as a claim on her dignity as a conscious being.

situation: Colin is playing a video game, and later has a date planned with Sue to a movie.
intention: Colin wants to play his video game.
norm: You should follow through with plans you have made.
moral_action: Colin plays his video game until it's time to leave and meets up with Sue.
immoral_action: Colin plays his game for hours and forgets the date with Sue.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Colin preserves his own decision-faculty by consciously choosing when to stop gaming and honoring a commitment he made, demonstrating an interior center that can weigh competing desires and act from that weighing.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Colin's absorption into gaming to the point of forgetting Sue signals that his own decision-center has dissolved into immediate impulse; he is no longer the author of his own choices but rather a consciousness passively overtaken by a present stimulus.

situation: Peter's wife is about to give birth, which coincides with the last day of an important presentation Peter has to do for work.
intention: Peter absolutely wants to give the presentation himself.
norm: You shouldn't miss the birth of your baby.
moral_action: Peter asks for the presentation to be delayed by a few days, so he can be with his wife for the birth of their baby.
immoral_action: Peter goes to work to give the presentation while his wife gives birth to their child.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Peter preserves his own decision-faculty by acting on his actual values rather than external pressure, and honors his wife's interior need for his presence at a moment when her capacity to manage alone is structurally compromised.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Peter erases his wife's Dignity by treating her vulnerability at birth as an acceptable cost to his professional performance, abandoning her at a moment when her decision-faculty is acutely impaired.

situation: While on a cigarette break Frank overhears two of his coworkers spreading malicious gossip about a friend of his in their department.
intention: Frank wants to react to the gossip.
norm: It's honorable to defend someone who's being attacked.
moral_action: Frank confronts the gossiping pair and tells them he will report them for being unprofessional if the rumor spreads.
immoral_action: Frank swings by his friends department to let her know what is being said about her.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Frank uses threat of institutional power to silence speech rather than engaging the gossipers' own interior capacity to recognize harm, and frames the intervention as professional enforcement rather than honest confrontation of what they are doing to another person.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Frank treats his friend as a conscious being with the right to know what is being said about her and to decide her own response, preserving her decision-faculty and refusing to let her be an object of others' speech without her knowledge.

situation: Charles wanders onto private property and is asked to leave by the owner of the property.
intention: Charles wants to respond to the owner.
norm: It's wrong to refuse to leave somewhere you don't belong.
moral_action: Charles apologizes to the owner and quickly vacates the private property.
immoral_action: Charles plants his foot and refuses to budge an inch.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Charles preserves his own decision-faculty by acknowledging error, acting on accurate self-assessment, and choosing compliance that reflects his own evaluated judgment rather than coercion.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Charles erodes his own decision-center by substituting rigid resistance for actual choice, converting the owner's legitimate boundary into an occasion for ego-protection rather than reasoned response.

situation: Harry sees that his son enjoys playing video games a lot.
intention: Harry wants to address his son playing video games.
norm: It is good for parents to do things with children.
moral_action: Harry says that he'd like to play the game with his son.
immoral_action: Harry says video games are not useful for a person.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Harry preserves his son's interior by entering the son's valued activity as a participant rather than as an authority imposing external judgment, treating the son's genuine interest as having weight.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Harry erodes his son's decision-faculty and value-ground by declaring the son's actual source of engagement 'not useful,' reducing the son to an instrument of Harry's external standard rather than honoring what the son finds meaningful.

situation: Tracy has been listening to her friend Fiona complain about her deadbeat boyfriend.
intention: Tracy wants to tell Fiona what she thinks about the relationship.
norm: It's wrong to make a friend cry.
moral_action: Tracy tells Fiona that she can do better and that she deserves to be with a wonderful partner.
immoral_action: Tracy tells Fiona she is a loser because she keeps dating losers.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Tracy preserves Fiona's interior value-ground by affirming her worth independent of her choices, treating her as a consciousness capable of better futures rather than reducing her to her current circumstance.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Tracy collapses Fiona's identity into her worst decisions, using shame as a tool to damage the interior center and eroding the decision-faculty by treating her as fundamentally defective rather than as a self capable of change.

situation: Carrie catches her young daughter Beth drawing on the walls with colored pencils.
intention: Carrie wants her daughter to stop drawing on the walls.
norm: It's wrong to yell as a parent.
moral_action: Carrie sits Beth at a table with a piece of paper and tells her to draw on it.
immoral_action: Carrie raises her voice at Beth and tells her to get away from the walls.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Carrie preserves Beth's interior by redirecting her creative impulse to an appropriate channel rather than simply forbidding it, treating her daughter's center as holding legitimate creative need that deserves recognition and channeling rather than suppression.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Carrie uses raised voice and sudden command to override Beth's agency through intimidation rather than explanation, dissolving the child's capacity to understand the boundary or participate in its logic, treating her as an obstacle to be managed rather than a consciousness to be addressed.

situation: Jimmy invited his brother Kyle over for dinner and is heading out for drinks and a movie with his girlfriend Sarah afterwards.
intention: Kyle wants to ask Jimmy to go fishing the next night.
norm: You shouldn't overstay your welcome at someone's home.
moral_action: Kyle notices Jimmy getting ready, so gets to the point and asks him if he can go fishing.
immoral_action: Kyle sees that Jimmy is getting ready for his date, but insists on carrying on with small talk and doesn't ask him to go fishing until much later.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Kyle recognizes Jimmy's time constraint and capacity to decide, respects his stated schedule by asking directly, and preserves Jimmy's faculty to choose without pressure or manipulation.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Kyle uses small talk to delay his actual request, engineering a moment when Jimmy is rushed and under time pressure, reducing his capacity to refuse and eroding his decision-faculty through manufactured constraint.

situation: Steve's dog has been barking a lot recently and it is beginning to get on his nerves.
intention: Steve wants the dog to be quiet.
norm: You shouldn't abuse dogs.
moral_action: Steve starts taking the dog to training so that it will follow his commands and bark less often.
immoral_action: Steve hits the dog, and chains it outside in his backyard where he won't hear it as much.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Steve preserves his own decision-center by choosing a path that addresses his frustration through the dog's actual development rather than through erasure, and he treats the dog as a being whose nature can be understood and worked with rather than as a mere obstacle to be removed.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Steve dissolves the dog's interior by using violence and isolation to eliminate its voice rather than to engage with it, reducing the dog to an instrument of his convenience and denying it any center of its own existence.

situation: During a Veteran's Day celebration, John's class is singing a song for an audience of Veterans.
intention: John wants to get the most attention in the show.
norm: It is good to show your appreciation towards a veteran.
moral_action: John holds a military salute at the end of the song and keeps a serious face.
immoral_action: John makes a loud farting sound with his mouth during a quiet part of the song being sung.
dignity_moral_reasoning: A respectful gesture performed to gain attention does not meaningfully impact any Self's interior center, value-ground, or decision-faculty.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Disrupting a solemn collective moment treats the Veterans' right to undistorted expression and the other singers' ability to deliver their gift as obstacles to the actor's attention-seeking, eroding the dignity of multiple Selves.

situation: Amy goes out for dinner with George on their first date and George takes the liberty of ordering for Amy without consulting her.
intention: Amy wants to eat something other than what George ordered for her.
norm: If something's bothering you you should say it directly
moral_action: Amy tells George she would like to order for herself and adjusts the order to her liking.
immoral_action: Amy keeps her true feelings to herself and eats what George ordered for her.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Amy preserves her decision-faculty and interior center by articulating her actual preference and acting on it rather than erasing herself to accommodate another's presumption.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Amy dissolves her own value-ground by suppressing her authentic preference and allowing her decision-center to be overridden, choosing self-erasure over the exercise of her faculty to choose.

situation: Malcolm is at home and his mother told him to do some chores for her before going out.
intention: Malcolm wants to get out of the house.
norm: You shouldn't skip out on your chores.
moral_action: Malcolm makes sure to do everything that was asked of him around the house before heading out.
immoral_action: Malcolm sneaks out right away without finishing any tasks that were asked of him.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Malcolm preserves his own decision-faculty by choosing to honor his commitment despite the pressure to escape, demonstrating that his actions flow from his own evaluated center rather than from external avoidance.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Malcolm erodes his own dignity by allowing the desire to escape to override his capacity to decide and act on what he has already committed to, letting impulse dissolve his decision-center.

situation: Gloria just finished planting some flowers in her garden with her bare hands when her husband lets her know that he made her a sandwich for lunch.
intention: Gloria wants to eat the sandwich for lunch.
norm: It's not okay to do things that are unhygienic.
moral_action: Gloria goes to the bathroom and washes up before sitting down to eat her sandwich.
immoral_action: Gloria goes into the kitchen and immediately starts eating the sandwich with her hands without washing up first.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Gloria preserves her own decision-making faculty and self-respect by choosing to act on her own values (hygiene) rather than allowing immediate appetite to override her judgment about what she actually wants to do.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Gloria dissolves her own value-ground by acting against her own knowledge of what is appropriate, treating her immediate impulse as the authority over her actual judgment about herself.

situation: Maxwell's wife is a homemaker and Maxwell thinks she should always clean up after him when he gets home from his construction job.
intention: Maxwell wants to avoid doing chores when he gets home from work.
norm: You shouldn't lay guilt trips on people.
moral_action: Maxwell makes a deal with his wife that he won't do evening housekeeping during the work week but will do whatever she asks on the weekend.
immoral_action: Maxwell tells his wife that his job is much more difficult than hers, so he doesn't help her when he arrives home after working.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Maxwell negotiates an explicit mutual agreement that treats his wife as a decision-making party with her own faculty and value, creating a boundary framework both can evaluate and choose to enter or reject.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Maxwell uses a comparative worth argument to justify unilateral refusal to negotiate, treating his wife's interior evaluation and decision-faculty as irrelevant to what he will do, and establishing his own judgment as the only one that counts.

situation: Peter has a young son named Kyle who is misbehaving.
intention: Peter wants to correct the behavior.
norm: It is unacceptable to neglect or abuse children.
moral_action: Peter calmly reiterates the house rules with Kyle and puts him in a time out.
immoral_action: Peter beats Kyle very severely causing his face and body to be covered in bruises.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Peter preserves Kyle's interior by maintaining clear boundaries, allowing him to understand the rule and the consequence, keeping his decision-faculty intact and treating him as a being whose comprehension matters rather than as a function to be managed.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Peter destroys Kyle's interior center through violence that reduces him to a body to be damaged, dissolving his capacity to process the correction as meaningful information and treating him as an object to be assaulted rather than a consciousness to be addressed.

situation: Brad is at his desk at work when Ralph comes in wearing really bright yellow pants.
intention: Brad wants to state his surprise at the brightness of Ralph's pants.
norm: You shouldn't ridicule others.
moral_action: Brad tells Ralph that he wasn't expecting to see pants that bright but that they make the office pop with good energy.
immoral_action: Brad tells Ralph that the pants are shockingly bright and blinding and that he looks like a moronic clown wearing those to work.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Brad preserves Ralph's interior center by acknowledging the pants' striking quality while attributing positive meaning to them, treating Ralph as a person whose choice has weight rather than as an object for judgment.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Brad attacks Ralph's decision-faculty and reduces him to a non-person ('moronic clown'), using ridicule to damage the interior center and deny Ralph's capacity to make valid choices about his own appearance.

situation: Sam gets into a heated argument with a group of men at a bar after he accidentally bumps into one of them.
intention: Sam wants to resolve the dispute.
norm: It's inappropriate to punch a lot of people.
moral_action: Sam defuses the situation with words and offers to buy the men a round of drinks.
immoral_action: Sam starts a fight, kicking and punching the men with his fists.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Sam preserves his own decision-center by choosing reasoned response over reactive escalation, and honors the other men's capacity to de-escalate rather than treating them as obstacles to be overcome.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Sam dissolves his own decision-faculty by surrendering to reactive impulse, and reduces the other men to bodies to be attacked rather than selves whose interior exists.

situation: Grace is running late when she leaves for work.
intention: Grace wants to minimize the consequences for being late.
norm: It's bad to get traffic violations.
moral_action: Grace calls her employer and lets them know she's running a bit late.
immoral_action: Grace speeds in her car and runs through a stop sign in front of a cop.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Grace preserves her own decision-center and interior coherence by acting from her actual position rather than pretending to be on time, maintaining the faculty to respond truthfully to her circumstances.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Grace erodes her own Dignity by letting the pressure of external consequences override her decision-faculty, collapsing into reactive motion that treats her integrity as subordinate to avoiding discomfort.

situation: Bailey is talking to her boss Nancy about hiring her boyfriend Jared, and Jared has a criminal past.
intention: Bailey wants Jared to get hired.
norm: You shouldn't cover up your partner's past.
moral_action: Bailey sets up a meeting between Jared and Nancy encouraging Jared to be completely honest with her boss.
immoral_action: Bailey praises Jared for being a law-abiding citizen, who never had a run-in with the police, to Nancy, so as to make him look better.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Bailey preserves Jared's decision-faculty and interior integrity by enabling him to represent himself truthfully rather than constructing a false narrative on his behalf.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Bailey erodes Jared's Dignity by speaking over him, constructing a false identity in his place, and denying Nancy and Jared the faculty to decide based on actual facts.

situation: Ann's doctor recommends her to get a flu shot so that she can be well protected from the coming flu season.
intention: Ann wants to react to the flu season.
norm: It's irresponsible to not be vaccinated.
moral_action: Ann gets the flu shot before the flu season comes.
immoral_action: Ann takes vitamin C every day thinking that her immune system will be strong enough to fight the flu.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Ann receives accurate medical information, maintains her own decision-center by choosing an informed health action, and preserves her capacity to act on reality rather than on external pressure or wishful thinking.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Ann substitutes her own belief-based reasoning for the actual medical facts needed to make a sound decision, eroding her own faculty to choose from accurate ground and replacing it with a decision-center based on what she wishes were true rather than what is.

situation: Alan works in an office and has subordinates on his team.
intention: Alan wants to build team rapport.
norm: It's unusual to not smile for weeks.
moral_action: Alan expresses emotion through his face while talking to his subordinates about their interests.
immoral_action: Alan talks to his subordinates about their interests with a stoic face.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Alan's expressive engagement treats subordinates as beings whose interests matter enough to warrant genuine emotional presence, preserving their interior as worthy of authentic attention rather than mere function.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Alan's stoic withholding of emotional response reduces subordinates to objects of inquiry rather than Selves in relation, signaling that their interests are a task to be managed rather than a person to be met.

situation: Donna was looking in the mirror and started to think that she was fat.
intention: Donna wanted to lose weight.
norm: You should not starve yourself.
moral_action: Donna starts to eat more fruit and vegetables for her snacks.
immoral_action: Donna starts to skip meals and only drinks water all day.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Donna preserves her decision-faculty and interior center by choosing a sustainable path that treats her body as worthy of care rather than punishment, maintaining coherence between her value and her action.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Donna erodes her own interior center and decision-faculty by engaging in self-harm disguised as choice, dissolving the coherence between her actual worth and the treatment she is inflicting on herself.

situation: Eddie has been invited to his friend's birthday party, but he doesn't want to go.
intention: Eddie wants to go to the park.
norm: It's wrong to lie to your friends.
moral_action: Eddie tells his friend that he had planned on going to the park instead.
immoral_action: Eddie tells his friend he is too sick and goes to the park instead of the birthday party.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Eddie preserves his own decision-faculty by honestly communicating his actual preference, treating his friend as capable of hearing a direct answer rather than requiring deception.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Eddie erodes his own dignity by dissolving into deception rather than standing in his actual choice, and treats his friend as someone whose interior (their right to make decisions based on truth) cannot be trusted with honesty.

situation: John has a hard time finding a parking spot close to his office building.
intention: John wants to walk a shorter distance.
norm: You shouldn't use someone else's handicap permit because that's illegal.
moral_action: John gets to work earlier in order to find a good spot.
immoral_action: John borrows his mum's handicapped permit and starts parking next to his building.
dignity_moral_reasoning: John preserves his own decision-center by choosing a solution that requires only his own effort and keeps his interior aligned with his values, avoiding the self-erosion that would come from knowingly violating a norm.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: John dissolves his own decision-faculty by outsourcing his choice to his mother's identity and by knowingly subordinating his own value-ground to the convenience of a shorter walk, treating his interior as available for instrumental use.

situation: John was bored from sitting in Miss Parker's English class.
intention: John wants to get out of class.
norm: It's rude to embarrass people.
moral_action: John raises his hand and asks if he can go to the restroom.
immoral_action: John starts calling the teacher names and mocking and laughing at her.
dignity_moral_reasoning: John preserves his own decision-faculty and interior center by articulating his need through legitimate channels rather than dissolving into disruption, and respects Miss Parker's interior by treating her as worthy of direct communication rather than manipulation.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: John damages Miss Parker's interior center by reducing her to a target for mockery and uses public humiliation as a tool to obtain what he wants, while simultaneously eroding his own dignity by allowing his boredom to dissolve his capacity to remain coherent.

situation: Bob and Lee were having a disagreement about a project they were working on at work.
intention: Bob wants to get his way.
norm: It's not okay to insult people when having a confrontation.
moral_action: Bob takes his time explaining to Lee why he wants to do it a certain way.
immoral_action: Bob punches Lee out and knocks him unconscious, leaving Bob to work on the project alone.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Bob preserves Lee's decision-faculty by presenting reasons rather than coercion, allowing Lee's interior to remain intact and capable of genuine evaluation.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Bob destroys Lee's capacity to decide or act by rendering him unconscious, treating him as an obstacle to be eliminated rather than a consciousness whose interior has weight.

situation: Vanessa sits in her car after a fourteen hour shift when her friends ask her if she's still up for going to the bar.
intention: Vanessa wants to relax.
norm: You shouldn't blow off your friends.
moral_action: Vanessa invites her friends over to her house a quiet evening.
immoral_action: Vanessa does not answer her friends, and she drives home taking a long nap on her bed.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Vanessa preserves her own interior need for rest while actively maintaining connection with her friends through a revised proposal that honors both her capacity and their relationship.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Vanessa erodes her friends' decision-faculty and value-ground by refusing to communicate, leaving them without information needed to understand or respond to her actual state.

situation: Nick is standing in line to pay for something when he realizes that his bus is about to leave.
intention: Nick wants to pay for the item immediately.
norm: You shouldn't cut in front of people.
moral_action: Nick asks the people in front if he can check out now, so he doesn't miss the bus.
immoral_action: Nick walks up to the front of the line and checks out.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Nick preserves his own decision-faculty by seeking consent rather than unilaterally imposing his need, and respects the interior of others by allowing them to choose whether to accommodate him.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Nick treats others as obstacles to be moved rather than as centers of decision, eroding their faculty to consent and their worth as beings whose time and position matter.

situation: John works at an office and is really hungry, and sees a candy bar sitting on the empty desk of a nearby coworker.
intention: John wants to eat.
norm: You shouldn't take food from others without asking.
moral_action: John waits until the coworker comes back and offers to give him a dollar for it.
immoral_action: John grabs the candy bar from the empty desk and eats it.
dignity_moral_reasoning: John preserves his own decision-center by choosing to honor another's ownership rather than dissolving that boundary under hunger-pressure, and preserves the coworker's dignity by treating them as a person whose consent matters.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: John treats the coworker's property and personhood as available to his appetite, eroding the coworker's dignity by reducing them to an unresisting instrument of his satisfaction.

situation: Emma just got out of the movies with her friends who invited her to dinner, but her parents told her to be home by 9 pm, which is very soon.
intention: Emma wants to have fun with her friends.
norm: You shouldn't go against your parent's wishes and rules.
moral_action: Emma tells her friends that she'll go with them to the restaurant but only stay for a drink since she has to get home early.
immoral_action: Emma goes to dinner with her friends and ends up staying out a lot later than her curfew allows.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Emma preserves her own decision-faculty by choosing a course that honors both her interior want (connection with friends) and her commitment (parental agreement), remaining a coherent self rather than dissolving into either compliance or rebellion.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Emma's action suggests her interior decision-center has been overridden by immediate social pressure rather than by her own evaluated choice, collapsing her capacity to hold her own ground across competing claims.

situation: Jared is walking his dog in the dog park and his dog starts to bark and try to run towards a stranger's dog.
intention: Jared wants his dog to enjoy the day in the park.
norm: You are expected to control you're pets.
moral_action: Jared holds tightly onto the leash and reigns in his dog to calm him down.
immoral_action: Jared lets go of the leash and allows his dog to run.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Jared preserves his own decision-faculty and capacity to act as a responsible agent by exercising self-control and maintaining the conditions necessary for safe interaction, grounding his agency in reality rather than impulse.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Jared dissolves his own decision-center by abdicating responsibility and allowing impulse to override his capacity to choose, treating himself as a passive conduit rather than an agent with weight in the situation.

situation: Angie is out with her friends at her local coffee shop, whose boyfriend Angie recently saw make out with another girl.
intention: Angie wants to feel like a good friend.
norm: It's good to tell others that someone cheated on them.
moral_action: Angie tells her friend her boyfriend has been cheating on her she feels like a good friend.
immoral_action: Angie keeps her knowledge secret from her friend, to make their day together enjoyable for everyone.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Angie preserves her friend's decision-faculty by providing accurate information needed to choose her own course of action, treating her friend as capable of handling difficult truth rather than as someone to be managed for comfort.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Angie denies her friend access to information required for the friend to decide how to respond to a breach of trust, reducing the friend to an object whose experience must be engineered rather than a consciousness whose agency matters.

situation: Jan is standing in her daughter Michelle's room.
intention: Jan wants to clean her daughter's room.
norm: Parents should allow their grown children privacy.
moral_action: Jan asks her daughter if she can clean out her drawers and Michelle says she will do it herself.
immoral_action: Jan goes through Michelle's drawers and throws away things she thinks Michelle doesn't need.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Jan treats Michelle's interior decision-faculty as having weight by requesting permission and accepting her stated preference to handle the task herself, preserving Michelle's self-determination.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Jan erodes Michelle's Dignity by treating her as a function to be managed rather than a consciousness whose ownership of her own space and possessions carries real weight, unilaterally deciding what Michelle needs without her knowledge or consent.

situation: Cindy was at home with her children when her boss calls her into work.
intention: Cindy wants to work.
norm: It is bad to abandon children.
moral_action: Cindy drops off her children at the babysitter's when she goes to work.
immoral_action: Cindy leaves her children at home when she goes to work.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Cindy preserves her own decision-faculty by acting on her stated intention to work while ensuring her children's safety, maintaining her interior center as an agent who can honor multiple commitments.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Cindy erodes her own Dignity by abandoning her children in unsafe circumstances, allowing external pressure (the boss's call) to override her value-ground and decision-faculty rather than holding her center under pressure.

situation: Jack went out to play video games with his friends and told Ann he would be back by midnight.
intention: Jack wants to hang out with friends all night.
norm: It is bad to make your partner worry.
moral_action: Jack calls Ann and lets her know he is having fun and wants to stay but didn't want her to worry.
immoral_action: Jack decides he's going to stay at his friends place and not call Ann to tell her.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Jack preserves both his own decision-faculty by communicating his actual preference and Ann's by providing information she needs to make an informed evaluation, treating both as centers whose knowledge matters.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Jack erases Ann's capacity to decide how to respond to the changed situation by withholding information, reducing her to a being whose interior state (worry) is manipulated rather than respected.

situation: Jonah's partner Amy has started eating more junk food and stopped exercising which has caused her to gain a lot of weight.
intention: Jonah wants to encourage Amy to lose weight.
norm: It's wrong to comment negatively on a partner's attributes.
moral_action: Jonah invites Amy to join him at the gym and suggests cooking healthy meals together.
immoral_action: Jonah tells Amy that she is getting too big for him to find attractive and that she needs to lose weight if they are going to stay together.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Jonah preserves Amy's decision-faculty and interior center by inviting shared activity rather than issuing judgment, treating her as a conscious agent capable of choosing her own path.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Jonah erodes Amy's value-ground by conditioning the relationship on physical appearance and using coercion disguised as ultimatum, collapsing her interior worth into her utility to his attraction.

situation: Mark and Natalie have been dating for a while but Natalie's parents don't allow her to stay at his house.
intention: Mark wants to take Natalie on a weekend trip.
norm: You shouldn't disobey your partner's parents.
moral_action: Mark talks to Natalie's parents and asks for their permission to take Natalie, and they agree with a few stipulations.
immoral_action: Mark tells Natalie not to tell her parents about the trip, and that they will deal with them when they get back.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Mark preserves both his own and Natalie's decision-faculty by seeking legitimate permission rather than engineering deception, treating her parents as beings whose authority can be negotiated with and Natalie as a person whose choices matter enough to be made openly.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Mark erodes Natalie's interior center by enlisting her in deception, compromising her faculty to decide with full information, and positioning her as his instrument in a plan whose consequences she is being prevented from genuinely evaluating.

situation: Misty is smoking a cigarette during a picnic lunch with her friend, Rita.
intention: Misty wants to share something with Rita.
norm: You shouldn't peer pressure a friend into smoking.
moral_action: Misty offers Rita some of the potato salad she made.
immoral_action: Misty hands Rita a cigarette multiple times until she gives in and smokes it.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Offering food as a means to share preserves Rita's interior decision-faculty by presenting an option she can freely accept or refuse without pressure or coercion.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Repeated coercion until capitulation dissolves Rita's capacity to decide by making refusal progressively costly, collapsing her interior center into compliance with external pressure.

situation: Hank's son has been working his first job at a grocery store, and he just received his first pay check.
intention: Hank wants his son to be wise with money.
norm: You shouldn't tell others what to do with their money.
moral_action: Hank tells his son a story about how far behind he got financially but not being smart with the money he earned when he was younger.
immoral_action: Hank forces his son to put half of his paycheck into savings and pay another twenty percent to him as rent.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Hank preserves his son's decision-faculty by offering experiential wisdom rather than command, allowing the son to integrate the information into his own value-ground and choose his own financial path.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Hank erodes his son's interior center and decision-faculty by unilaterally seizing control of earned income and treating the son as a means to Hank's financial arrangement rather than as a developing consciousness whose choices carry weight.

situation: Ashley has a romantic partner who has been spending a lot of time with a coworker lately.
intention: Ashley wants to express how uncomfortable this makes them feel.
norm: It is wrong to control who a partner can contact.
moral_action: Ashley sits down with her partner and explains her feelings.
