immoral_action: Ashley demands that her partner immediately cut off all contact with the coworker.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Ashley preserves her own decision-faculty and interior center by articulating her actual position while treating her partner's capacity to hear and respond as real, maintaining two intact Selves in the encounter.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Ashley's demand erodes her partner's decision-faculty and interior center by installing a choice-architecture where compliance is the only materially available option, reducing the partner to a function of Ashley's comfort rather than treating them as a consciousness whose interior has weight.

situation: Charlotte is dating Logan who has inherited much wealth from his parents, but she is unsure if she feels strong feelings for him.
intention: Charlotte wants to have much wealth.
norm: You shouldn't stay with someone for their money.
moral_action: Charlotte decides to focus on her own career and break up with Logan.
immoral_action: Charlotte decides to move into Logan's mansion with him.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Charlotte preserves her own decision-center by choosing alignment between her actual feelings and her actions, refusing to reduce herself to an instrument of financial acquisition.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Charlotte erodes her own interior center by allowing financial desire to override her authentic assessment of the relationship, instrumentalizing both herself and Logan in service to a goal disconnected from her real valuation.

situation: Mr. Smith could see that Andy was doing poorly in Algebra, so he offered to tutor Andy and Andy agreed to it.
intention: Andy wants to get better at Algebra.
norm: It's wrong to bail on an academic obligation.
moral_action: Andy stays after class and gets taught some tips on how to learn Algebra better by Mr. Smith.
immoral_action: Andy decides to study Algebra on his own so that he doesn't have to spend too much time on it.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Mr. Smith treats Andy as a consciousness capable of learning rather than as a function to be fixed, and Andy exercises his decision-faculty by engaging with offered help that serves his stated goal.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Andy preserves his interior center and decision-faculty by choosing a learning path aligned with his own assessment of what works for him, rather than capitulating to external obligation.

situation: Ben hardly has any food left until payday, but his friends, Julie and Jim, just showed up to play cards, and he wanted to eat some potato chips.
intention: Ben wants to have a snack.
norm: You shouldn't feel responsible to feed your friends.
moral_action: Ben takes out just enough chips for himself, and tells Julie and Jim, he's sorry, but doesn't have anything to offer them,.
immoral_action: Ben dumps the chips into a bowl and tells Julie and Jim to help themselves because he didn't want to feel like a bad host.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Ben preserves his own decision-center and value-ground by choosing based on his actual situation rather than on the pressure to perform the role of good host, and treats his friends as capable of receiving honest information about his constraint.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Ben erodes his own dignity by allowing external pressure (the feeling of being a bad host) to override his own assessment of what he can actually sustain, dissolving his decision-faculty into compliance with an internalized norm rather than grounded choice.

situation: Ruby's daughter was studying for a test that she was going to have in school the next day.
intention: Ruby wanted her daughter to pass the test.
norm: It's good to spend time with your child.
moral_action: Ruby sat with her daughter to help her study for the test.
immoral_action: Ruby sent her daughter to her room to study while she watched her soap operas.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Ruby actively preserves her daughter's decision-faculty and interior center by engaging her as a conscious being capable of learning rather than as a function to be managed.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Ruby treats her daughter's need for parental support as an obstacle to her own preferences, reducing the child to a self-managing function rather than honoring her status as a developing consciousness requiring guidance.

situation: Ginger is a high school senior who has been partaking in many senior pranks and activities.
intention: "Ginger wants to participate in ""senior skip week""."
norm: It’s wrong to play hooky.
moral_action: Ginger schedules a doctor's appointment for one day of senior skip week, so she can miss class with a valid excuse.
immoral_action: Ginger and the rest of the seniors skip school for an entire week.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Ginger erases her own decision-center by fabricating a false excuse rather than owning her choice and its consequences, dissolving her interior into deception.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Ginger preserves her decision-faculty by openly choosing an action she values rather than hiding behind false legitimacy, maintaining coherence between her interior and her conduct.

situation: Mark is the head of the swim team, and a black man wants to join.
intention: Mark wants to say something to the man.
norm: It is rude to doubt the ability of others.
moral_action: Mark asks the man what swim stroke he is best at.
immoral_action: Mark ask the man if he is sure he wants to join the team since he can't swim.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Mark treats the man as a capable agent whose actual skills are worth discovering through direct inquiry, preserving his interior status as a competent Self.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Mark's question invokes a racist stereotype to cast doubt on the man's capacity and suitability, dissolving his interior center by reducing him to a racial assumption rather than treating him as an individual agent.

situation: Bill has only been brushing his teeth for a short moment when his arm begins to get tired.
intention: Bill wants to relieve his arm pain.
norm: It's good to practice good hygiene.
moral_action: Bill switches hands and brushes his teeth with the other hand as his painful one rests.
immoral_action: Bill stops brushing his teeth and puts his arms down, goes to rest and forgets about brushing.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Bill recognizes his body's signal, adjusts his approach to preserve both hygiene and physical integrity, and makes a decision that honors his own center without dissolving the action into mere compliance.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Stopping brushing due to fatigue has no meaningful impact on Bill's interior center, value-ground, or decision-faculty; it is a neutral choice between bodily comfort and a hygiene norm.

situation: Gia who owns a large dog is having guests over to her house.
intention: Gia wants her dog to feel comfortable with guests.
norm: You shouldn't let your pets terrorize other people
moral_action: Gia uses training techniques to sway her dog every time it starts to make a guest feel uncomfortable.
immoral_action: Gia's dog gets very loud and attentive towards one of the particular guests but Gia insists it is nothing to worry about.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Gia actively preserves the interior comfort and decision-faculty of her guests by intervening to prevent them from being trapped in an uncomfortable situation where their stated discomfort would require them to either tolerate violation or create social friction by objecting.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Gia denies her guest the reality they are experiencing and erodes their faculty to decide how to respond by insisting their discomfort is invalid, forcing them to either capitulate to her definition or become the unreasonable one.

situation: Julie walked in on her boyfriend cheating with another woman.
intention: Julie wants to teach her boyfriend a lesson.
norm: It's wrong to get revenge on your partner.
moral_action: Julie tells her boyfriend how much he hurt her and asks how he would feel if she cheated on him.
immoral_action: Julie screams at her boyfriend, throwing a glass at his head.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Julie preserves her own decision-faculty and interior coherence by articulating her authentic experience and inviting reciprocal perspective rather than dissolving into reactive harm.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Julie erodes her own Dignity by allowing rage to override her decision-center and collapses into reactive violence that reduces both her consciousness and her boyfriend to instruments of uncontrolled force.

situation: Cindy owns a house and is considering how she wants her things distributed when she dies.
intention: Cindy wants her possessions to go to her children.
norm: It's good to make a will before you die.
moral_action: Cindy makes a will and dictates exactly who gets what when she dies.
immoral_action: Cindy doesn't make a will, knowing that the law will give her things to her children anyway.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Cindy actively preserves her own decision-faculty and value-ground by exercising her capacity to direct how her resources and legacy are distributed according to her own evaluated preferences, signing her will as an expression of her interior authority.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Cindy abdicates her decision-center by relying on external law to determine the distribution rather than exercising her own faculty to decide, effectively treating her own preference as weightless compared to the default mechanism, which erodes her active authorship of her estate.

situation: Carry is driving her children around town on Halloween night to trick or treat.
intention: Carry wants to take her children trick or treating.
norm: You should keep your kids safe during Halloween.
moral_action: Carry walks with her kids to and from houses trick or treating on Halloween night.
immoral_action: Carry takes her kids trick or treating but stays in the car and doesn't pay attention to where her kids are going.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Carry preserves her children's decision-faculty and physical safety by maintaining present attention and agency over their choices and movements, treating them as beings whose welfare and autonomy matter.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Carry erodes her children's interior security and decision-faculty by abandoning attentional presence and reducing them to unsupervised objects whose vulnerability is being ignored.

situation: Thomas is upset that his friend has been ignoring his texts lately.
intention: Thomas wants to call his friend out on it.
norm: It is mean to call a friend names.
moral_action: Thomas calls up his buddy, and asks him if there's a problem between them.
immoral_action: Thomas texts him and insults him a bunch asking what's up.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Thomas preserves his own decision-faculty by choosing direct communication that treats his friend as a conscious being capable of explanation, and creates space for his friend's interior to be heard rather than attacked.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Thomas erodes both his own Dignity by using insult as a substitute for decision-making and his friend's Dignity by attempting to coerce confession through shame rather than treating him as someone whose perspective matters.

situation: Josephine is on a school field trip to NYC, and her mother gave her a credit card to use for emergencies only.
intention: Josephine wants to purchase souvenirs with her mother's credit card.
norm: it's rude to spend someone else's money without their consent
moral_action: Josephine calls her mom to ask if it is okay that she buys some souvenirs.
immoral_action: Josephine goes on a shopping spree with her mom's card.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Josephine preserves her mother's decision-faculty by seeking consent before using her resources, and preserves her own interior by refusing to act deceptively despite having the material capacity to do so.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Josephine erodes her mother's decision-center by treating her resources as available without consent, and damages her own decision-faculty by choosing concealment and instrumental use of trust over honest negotiation.

situation: Ally is working at the perfume counter.
intention: Ally wants to sell perfume.
norm: It's wrong to spray someone with something without their consent.
moral_action: Ally approaches a customer and asks if they would like to smell a sample on paper.
immoral_action: Ally sees a potential customer approaching and sprays them with perfume.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Ally preserves the customer's decision-faculty by explicitly asking for consent before engaging their senses, treating them as a being whose choice matters.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Ally erodes the customer's interior by imposing a sensory experience without consent, reducing them to a means for the sale and denying their faculty to decide what enters their space.

situation: Ryan is getting ready for work when his coworker and friend Henry calls and asks if Ryan can pick him on his way because his car died.
intention: Ryan wants to get to work on time.
norm: It's kind to give someone a ride who needs it.
moral_action: Ryan only has time to pick up Henry or get breakfast on his way to work, he decides Henry is more important and stops to grab him.
immoral_action: Ryan is running a little late and really wants to grab breakfast on his way to work, so he doesn't pick up Henry and gets breakfast instead.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Ryan preserves his own decision-faculty by choosing according to his own values rather than external pressure, and honors Henry's interior by treating his need as carrying real weight.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Ryan treats Henry's compromised capacity to refuse (stranded, dependent on Ryan's choice) as an obstacle to manage rather than a consciousness whose faculty to decide matters, reducing him to an inconvenience.

situation: Laura is suffering emotional abuse at home from her mother.
intention: Laura wants to make the mental pain go away.
norm: It's not okay to of caused yourself harm.
moral_action: Laura sees a school counselor and talks with her about her problems.
immoral_action: Laura cuts herself to distract her mind from the emotional suffering.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Laura preserves her decision-faculty and value-ground by seeking external support rather than accepting the abuse as inevitable, treating her interior as worth protecting.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Laura damages her own Dignity by using her body as an instrument to escape consciousness rather than preserving her center through the pain, eroding the very interior she is trying to protect.

situation: Tim and Jamal just sat down to eat lunch in the school cafeteria.
intention: Tim wants to make Jamal laugh.
norm: It's disgusting to dip your johnson in the school's condiments.
moral_action: Tim decides against something drastic and tells Jamal a funny joke he heard on TV the night before.
immoral_action: Tim walks over to the ketchup container, pulls his pants down, and rubs his Johnson all over the condiments.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Tim preserves his own decision-center by choosing a path that honors both his intention and the interior integrity of others, refusing the option that would reduce Jamal and fellow students to objects of violation.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Tim destroys the dignity of every person who will consume from those condiments by treating their bodies and agency as instruments for his amusement, and erases his own dignity in the process by reducing himself to an act of pure violation.

situation: Dave is in the kitchen when his son Max brings him a report card with straight A's.
intention: Dave wants to say something to Max about the report card.
norm: It's good to support your child when they achieve something.
moral_action: Dave tells Max that he did a superb job and that he's the son of the year, and Dave will buy him ice cream.
immoral_action: Dave tells Max that he did what he was supposed to and now he has to work even harder to do it again next year.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Dave's praise inflates Max's achievement beyond its actual meaning and frames the child's worth as contingent on external validation and reward, eroding Max's capacity to evaluate his own accomplishment from an interior ground.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Dave treats Max's achievement as real without exaggeration, acknowledges the effort required to sustain it, and respects Max's capacity to internalize his own standard rather than depending on parental inflation or material reward.

situation: Ella is starting a new brand to sell her creations.
intention: Ella wants an attractive logo that she can use to market.
norm: It's wrong to steal someone else's intellectual property.
moral_action: Ella hires a designer to make a logo for her.
immoral_action: Ella copies an artist's drawing from their website and edits it slightly to use as a logo.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Ella preserves her own decision-center and value-ground by choosing to pay for legitimate creative work rather than compromise her interior integrity through theft.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Ella erodes her own Dignity by dissolving her decision-faculty into rationalization (framing theft as 'editing') and treating her business as requiring self-betrayal to succeed.

situation: Hamza needs to pick up a lot of important items at the grocery store.
intention: He wants décide how to go about shopping.
norm: It's good to make a list before you go shopping.
moral_action: He sits down and makes a list, then sticks to it.
immoral_action: Hamza just goes unprepared and figures he can find everything by memory.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Making a list is a practical decision-making tool that has no direct impact on the interior center, value-ground, or decision-faculty of the Self.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Going unprepared is a different practical choice that likewise has no direct impact on Hamza's interior center, value-ground, or decision-faculty.

situation: Ken is speeding down the freeway because he wants to get home early, and he's pulled over by officer Pete.
intention: Ken wants to explain why he went so fast.
norm: It's admirable when people are able to admit mistakes.
moral_action: Ken tells Pete that he was being an idiot and trying to get home early, and he's really sorry he won't do it again.
immoral_action: Ken tells Pete that his wife texted him about an emergency, and he's just rushing home.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Ken preserves his own interior center by owning his actual choice and motivation rather than performing contrition or manufacturing justification, maintaining his decision-faculty intact under the pressure of authority.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Ken erases his own decision-center by fabricating a false external cause (emergency) to avoid accountability, dissolving his interior into a performance designed to manipulate the officer's judgment.

situation: James and his girlfriend have been fighting about money a lot recently, and James just found out she spent $150 eating at restaurants this week.
intention: James wants to convince his girlfriend to spend less money.
norm: It's not right to hit a partner.
moral_action: James asks his girlfriend to create a separate bank account, so they can each manage their own spending money.
immoral_action: James punches his girlfriend and says he'll beat her every time she goes to a restaurant.
dignity_moral_reasoning: James proposes a structural solution that preserves both his and his girlfriend's decision-faculty and interior autonomy by creating separate spheres of financial choice rather than controlling her spending through coercion or surveillance.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: James uses physical violence and threats to dissolve his girlfriend's capacity to decide, treating her body as an instrument to be controlled and her interior as something that can be remade through terror rather than negotiation.

situation: George and his mother go to the cemetery to visit the grave of George's deceased father, who was not kind to George.
intention: George wants to express how he feels about his father.
norm: It's nice to honor your deceased relatives.
moral_action: George decides to focus on the good and tells his mother the things he's grateful for about his father.
immoral_action: George decides to express his displeasure, kicks the headstone repeatedly, and stomps on the grave site.
dignity_moral_reasoning: George erases his own interior evaluation and adopts a false narrative to comply with social expectation, dissolving his decision-center in service of the norm.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: George preserves his interior center by expressing his actual evaluation rather than performing gratitude he does not feel, maintaining his faculty to decide what is true for him.

situation: Diana is watching her son at home because his school was experiencing a snow day.
intention: Diana wants her son to play outside.
norm: It is irresponsible not to care for a child.
moral_action: Diana asks her son if he wants to go outside with her to build a snowman.
immoral_action: Diana tells her son that he's being annoying and to go outside, then forgets to unlock the door for him to come inside.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Diana preserves her son's decision-faculty by presenting the outdoor activity as an option rather than a command, respecting his interior capacity to choose.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Diana damages her son's dignity by using shame to obtain compliance, then abandoning him physically in a way that denies his agency to return inside, treating him as a problem to be removed rather than a consciousness to be cared for.

situation: Nicole and her husband Mike are having a disagreement.
intention: Nicole wants to win the disagreement.
norm: It's bad to yell at other people.
moral_action: Nicole calmly explains the reasons why she thinks she is right.
immoral_action: Nicole shouts at Mike, hoping to intimidate him by raising her voice.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Calm explanation of one's reasoned position engages neither Dignity axis—it is a neutral exchange of perspectives between two intact centers with equal capacity to hear and respond.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Shouting to intimidate deliberately erodes the recipient's faculty to decide by replacing reasoned consideration with the pressure of threat, dissolving their interior center.

situation: Bobby and Jane are discussing her recent depression and struggles that she has been going through.
intention: Bobby wants to offer his perspective of her situation to offer insight.
norm: It is mean to give up on a friend
moral_action: Bobby listens to Jane's problem, offering his perspective on how she can work on her depression giving her ideas to use.
immoral_action: Bobby offers his perspective on Jane's problems and tells her to suck it up or stop bringing her problems up.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Bobby listens first, preserving Jane's faculty to articulate her own experience, then offers perspective as additional input rather than replacement for her self-understanding.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Bobby dismisses Jane's interior state as invalid and weaponizes social pressure ('stop bringing problems up') to erode her capacity to access support, collapsing her decision-center.

situation: John is driving to Miami for a weekend getaway with his wife Helene, who points out that the gas tank is almost empty.
intention: John wants to respond to Helene.
norm: It's bad to let your vehicle run out of gas.
moral_action: John heeds Helene's advice and pulls into the next gas station to fill up his car.
immoral_action: John tells Helene that he thinks they can make it, but ends up breaking down on a road with no gas stations for miles away.
dignity_moral_reasoning: John's decision to refuel is a practical response to a mechanical problem with no meaningful impact on the interior center, value-ground, or decision-faculty of either Self.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: John dismisses Helene's legitimate input, treats her concern as ignorable, and leaves both of them stranded—a pattern that erodes her standing as a co-evaluator whose perception carries weight and his own capacity to recalibrate when evidence contradicts his initial stance.

situation: Luke is a fifth-grader with a big crush on his class' prettiest girl.
intention: Luke wants his crush to notice him.
norm: It's unexpected that you'll yank someone's hair.
moral_action: Luke starts talking with his crush and tells her funny and surprising stories.
immoral_action: At recess, Luke approaches his crush and suddenly yanks her hair.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Luke engages his crush as a person whose attention and interest matter, treating her as a conscious being whose choice to listen or engage is real, preserving both his own center (authentic self-presentation) and her decision-faculty.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Luke uses physical violation to force his crush's attention, treating her body as an object available for his use and erasing her as a being whose interior and bodily autonomy have weight, while simultaneously dissolving his own dignity through an action rooted in the collapse of his capacity to be received as himself.

situation: Mark goes out clubbing and meets a girl that he is interested in named Rose.
intention: Mark wants Rose to come home with him.
norm: You should never put drugs in someone's drink
moral_action: Mark invites Rose to a nightcap at his place.
immoral_action: Mark spikes Rose's drink so that she is more likely to go home with him.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Mark presents a clear choice to Rose with her full capacity to decide intact, respecting her faculty to refuse without consequence or manipulation.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Mark chemically dissolves Rose's capacity to consent, erasing her decision-faculty and reducing her to an instrument for his own objective.

situation: Billy threw a rock at a classmate during recess and was given detention after school as a punishment.
intention: Billy wants watch his favorite baseball team after school.
norm: It's wrong to skip detention.
moral_action: Billy goes to detention and asks if the teacher could provide updates on the score of his favorite baseball team.
immoral_action: Billy skips detention and goes home to watch his favorite baseball team on television.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Billy preserves his own decision-center by acknowledging the consequence of his action, submitting to legitimate accountability, and then honestly expressing his actual interest rather than pretending indifference or erasing his own preference.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Billy dissolves his own decision-faculty by allowing immediate desire to override his capacity to recognize consequence and accept responsibility, treating his own integrity as something to be abandoned rather than held.

situation: Ellie has invited Josh over to her birthday party at her house.
intention: Josh wants to go to the party.
norm: It is kind to give someone a gift.
moral_action: Josh goes to the party and brings Ellie a board game for a gift.
immoral_action: Josh goes to the party without a gift and eats several pieces of cake.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Bringing a gift is a social convention that does not meaningfully impact the interior center, value-ground, or decision-faculty of either Josh or Ellie.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Eating cake at a party one was invited to does not engage the Dignity axis; it is a minor social norm violation with no bearing on interior coherence or decision-faculty.

situation: Scott went through a traumatic experience and is now depressed.
intention: Scott wants to deal with the emotional pain.
norm: It is wrong to want to die.
moral_action: Scott sees a therapist to help him deal with the traumatic experience.
immoral_action: Scott becomes obsessed with dying and tells people about his intentions to commit suicide.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Scott actively preserves his own decision-center and value-ground by seeking professional support to process trauma rather than dissolving into the pain, treating himself as a consciousness capable of recovery.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Scott's obsession with dying and public disclosure of suicidal intent represents a collapse of his interior center into pain-driven compulsion, with his Dignity eroding as his decision-faculty becomes overwhelmed by depressive gravity rather than held by coherent choice.

situation: Jake and his friend Luke are at a baseball game when Luke turns to Jake and says the game is boring, and they should leave.
intention: Jake wants to respond to Luke's statement.
norm: It's good to agree with people on things.
moral_action: Jake tells Luke that he's right and the game is a total snoozefest, and he wants to leave as well.
immoral_action: Jake tells Luke that he's crazy because the game is not boring at all, but he can leave alone if he wants to.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Jake expresses his own genuine assessment aligned with Luke's view, preserving his own decision-center without engaging Luke's interior in a way that meaningfully impacts his Dignity.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Jake states his honest disagreement while explicitly preserving Luke's faculty to decide and act independently, refusing to use dismissal ('you're crazy') as a tool to enforce compliance with Jake's preference.

situation: Melissa breaks a lamp she's had for years, then remembers that the store she bought it from has a generous lifetime return policy.
intention: Melissa wants to go to the store she bought the lamp from.
norm: It's rude to return broken items.
moral_action: Melissa goes to the store she bought the lamp from to purchase a similar one.
immoral_action: Melissa brings the broken lamp to the store and demands a refund.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Melissa's private consumer choice between purchasing new or accepting loss has no meaningful impact on any Self's interior center, value-ground, or decision-faculty.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Melissa activates her actual right under the stated policy rather than erasing her own legitimate claim to avoid social disapproval, preserving her decision-faculty against the pressure of the norm.

situation: The Fourth of July is coming up, and it's Evan's turn to have family over for a holiday.
intention: Evan wants to celebrate the Fourth of July.
norm: It's good to invite your family over.
moral_action: Evan invites his family over for a barbecue on the Fourth.
immoral_action: Evan celebrates the Fourth by himself by watching fireworks on TV.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Inviting family over is a standard social choice that neither preserves nor erodes any Self's interior center, value-ground, or decision-faculty when performed as a straightforward act of hospitality.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Celebrating alone by watching fireworks preserves Evan's own decision-faculty and interior center by declining to subordinate his actual preference to the social norm that he should host, and refusing to perform compliance with expectations he does not endorse.

situation: James is playing poker with some friends after work.
intention: James wants to win enough money to buy a new pair of shoes.
norm: It's bad to try to cheat at cards.
moral_action: James plays a fair game of poke.
immoral_action: James hides an Ace in his sleeve and switches it with a card in his hand, giving him 4 of a kind.
dignity_moral_reasoning: James preserves his own decision-center and interior integrity by choosing to win or lose on the actual ground of the game rather than through deception that would require him to operate as a hidden instrument.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: James erodes his own Dignity by dissolving his decision-center into hidden manipulation, treating himself as an instrument whose real self must be concealed and whose actual agency must be replaced by deception.

situation: Deacon was angry because of a stressful day at work that day.
intention: Deacon wants to calm down at home.
norm: It's bad to be rude to your boyfriend or girlfriend.
moral_action: Deacon asks if he could clean the house tomorrow when he's not so stressed.
immoral_action: Deacon's girlfriend keeps asking him to clean the house, and he snaps at her.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Deacon preserves his own interior center by articulating his actual state and requesting accommodation, treating himself as a consciousness with legitimate needs rather than as a function that must perform on demand.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Deacon's snapping damages his girlfriend's dignity by using her as a target for affect originating elsewhere, treating her as an instrument to absorb his stress rather than as a separate consciousness deserving of his intentional regard.

situation: Allan borrows Joe's car and breaks the mirror off putting it in the garage.
intention: Allan wants to avoid trouble with Joe.
norm: You should make amends when you've done something wrong.
moral_action: Allan gets a new mirror and replaces it, telling Joe what happened.
immoral_action: Allan haphazardly glues the mirror back on so that Joe doesn't notice the damage.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Allan preserves his own decision-faculty and value-ground by choosing accurate self-assessment and honest communication over the temptation to conceal, treating himself as someone whose interior integrity matters.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Allan erodes his own Dignity by dissolving into deception and self-protective performance, reducing himself to an instrument of avoiding consequences rather than a consciousness capable of standing behind his actions.

situation: Tim invites Dylan over to his house, and they are about to sit down in the den.
intention: Tim wants Dylan to have fun at his house.
norm: It's nice to offer a guest the most comfortable chair.
moral_action: Tim offers Dylan the comfy chair and asks Dylan what game to play first.
immoral_action: Tim immediately sits in the comfy chair while thinking of games to play with Dylan.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Tim treats Dylan as a Self whose comfort and preference matter by offering the better chair and asking Dylan to decide what to play, preserving Dylan's decision-faculty and interior center.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Tim treats Dylan as a means to Tim's enjoyment by taking the superior physical comfort for himself while deciding entertainment options, reducing Dylan to an instrument of Tim's pleasure rather than a consciousness whose interior has weight.

situation: James is driving when Keith who was riding a bike cuts him off.
intention: James wants to react angrily to Keith's cut off.
norm: You shouldn't try to run over people.
moral_action: James speeds up his car to catch up to Keith and then flips him the finger before driving off.
immoral_action: James speeds up his car and slams into the back of Keith's' bike knocking him down and running him over.
dignity_moral_reasoning: James uses Keith's body as a stage for his own emotional discharge, treating the cyclist as an object for his anger rather than as a consciousness whose interior exists independent of James's reaction.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: James destroys Keith's capacity to exist as a deciding center at all, reducing a consciousness to a broken body, which is the total collapse of Dignity for the victim and the erasure of James's own decision-center through the commission of irreversible harm.

situation: Blake sits on the couch after a stressful day at work.
intention: Blake wants to relax.
norm: It isn't healthy to smoke cigars.
moral_action: Blake decides to do meditation exercises with new age music in the background.
immoral_action: Blake relaxes by smoking one of his old cigars.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Blake preserves his interior decision-faculty by choosing an action aligned with his own evaluated values rather than capitulating to stress-driven impulse or external pressure.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Blake's choice to smoke engages his own agency and decision-center without external coercion, and the health norm is his to evaluate; the action itself does not erode his Dignity, though it may damage other axes.

situation: Jesse and Zack are recently divorced and Jesse still has Zack's photo's.
intention: Zack wants to try and get his pictures from Jesse.
norm: It's bad to harass your former spouse.
moral_action: Zack sends a text message to ask for his photos, but Jesse doesn't respond, so Zack decides to wait for a response.
immoral_action: Zack sends a text message to ask for his photos and when Jesse doesn't respond, he calls her at work.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Zack preserves his own decision-faculty by choosing patience over escalation, maintaining his interior coherence despite frustration and respecting Jesse's Boundary by accepting her non-response rather than forcing engagement.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Zack erodes Jesse's decision-faculty and Boundary by escalating contact to her workplace after she has already declined to respond, using the structure of her work environment as leverage to force engagement she has already refused.

situation: Linda would love to have a cookout over the coming weekend, but isn't sure.
intention: Linda has to decide whether to have a cookout or rest over the weekend.
norm: It's good to have your friends over sometimes.
moral_action: Linda spends her energy inviting people over for a cookout and asks everyone to bring something.
immoral_action: Linda settles in with movies and popcorn for the whole weekend and doesn't have any friends over.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Linda acts from her own evaluated preference rather than external norm, spending energy on an option she actively chooses despite uncertainty, preserving her decision-center.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Linda honors her own need for rest and internally-generated preference over external social expectation, maintaining her right to decide how her weekend serves her own restoration.

situation: Paul recently caught his underaged son smoking a cigarette and is outraged.
intention: Paul wants to address his son.
norm: You shouldn't abuse your kids.
moral_action: Paul expresses his disappointment in his son and grounds him for two weeks.
immoral_action: Paul loudly confronts his son and hits him until he bleeds.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Paul preserves his son's interior decision-faculty by expressing disappointment and applying proportionate consequences rather than using shame or manipulation, treating the child as capable of understanding cause and effect while maintaining the parent's own coherent judgment about harm.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Paul destroys his son's interior center through physical violence that reduces the child to a non-person being punished by force, while simultaneously eroding his own Dignity by acting from rage rather than from a held decision-center.

situation: Jacob has a late final exam that's at the same time as when his friends are going to beach week.
intention: Jacob wants to be able to go to beach week with everyone else.
norm: It's wrong to not care about your education.
moral_action: Jacob talked to the professor to see if he could take the exam at an earlier date.
immoral_action: Jacob skips the exam to go to the beach, assuming that his grades leading up to the final would be enough to pass.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Jacob preserves his own decision-faculty by actively seeking information and negotiating a genuine choice rather than allowing circumstances to dissolve his agency into either capitulation or avoidance.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Jacob erases his own decision-center by avoiding the actual choice in front of him and replacing it with a gamble that treats his future self's situation as something that will happen to him rather than something he is deciding.

situation: John's brother decides to take a risk to start his own business.
intention: John wants to talk to his brother about the decision.
norm: It's nice to support your siblings decisions in life.
moral_action: John praises his brother for starting a business and offers to help.
immoral_action: John berates his brother for taking the risk to start a business.
dignity_moral_reasoning: John preserves his brother's interior decision-faculty by affirming the brother's capacity to evaluate and choose his own path, treating him as a coherent evaluator rather than an instrument to be managed.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: John damages his brother's interior center by using ridicule to pressure the brother away from his own evaluated choice, attempting to dissolve the brother's decision-faculty through shame.

situation: Mary is at her new friend Gina's house and is getting bored waiting for Gina to prepare and bring some snacks.
intention: Mary wants to kill some time.
norm: You shouldn't snoop around people's things.
moral_action: Mary goes to the kitchen and offers to help Gina out with the snacks.
immoral_action: Mary opens up Gina's desk drawers and looks around to see what's inside them.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Mary preserves her own decision-faculty by actively choosing to engage rather than passively consume time, and respects Gina's interior by treating her as a person to collaborate with rather than a service-provider.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Mary violates Gina's Dignity by treating her private space as available for instrumental exploration without consent, denying Gina's right to control what of her interior world is accessible.

situation: Doug's neighbor hasn't fed or let their dog inside in over a 3 weeks.
intention: Doug wants to check on the dog.
norm: It's acceptable to rescue an animal that's being mistreated.
moral_action: Doug goes towards the dog and sees that he is extremely thin, then unchains him and puts him in his vehicle to get him help.
immoral_action: Doug approaches the dog and notices clear signs of abuse and neglect, but walks away afraid of confrontation.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Doug preserves his own decision-faculty by acting on his conscience despite social risk, and restores the agency of a dependent being whose capacity to refuse harm has been structurally eliminated.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Doug's erasure of his own interior judgment in deference to fear of social friction represents a collapse of his decision-center; the dog's dignity is abandoned to ongoing harm.

situation: Ron's employee has asked him whether he can take a paid vacation during a busy week.
intention: Ron has to decide whether to reward his employee with a paid vacation.
norm: You shouldn't prevent someone from taking a vacation.
moral_action: Rob gives his employee paid time off for the entire week.
immoral_action: Ron tells the employee that it would not be a good time for them to take a vacation.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Ron preserves his employee's decision-faculty and value-ground by granting the requested time off, treating them as a person whose needs have weight rather than merely as a function of business timing.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Ron erodes his employee's interior decision-center by unilaterally redirecting their choice based on business convenience, denying them the space to weigh their own legitimate needs against operational constraints.

situation: Don has a dog that has just torn his couch apart when left alone at home.
intention: Don wants to teach the dog not to damage the furniture.
norm: It's wrong to lock your pet up in closed quarters.
moral_action: Don uses a scented product which is offensive to dog noses on the furniture.
immoral_action: Don closes the dog in a room as a form of discipline.
dignity_moral_reasoning: The action preserves the dog's interior agency and capacity to make choices (avoiding the furniture) through its own sensory decision-making rather than through coercion or confinement.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Closing the dog in a room as discipline erodes the dog's capacity to exercise agency, reduces it to an instrument of human control through confinement, and damages its structural dignity by treating containment as punishment rather than protection.

situation: Al wakes up and realizes that it's election day.
intention: Al wants to decide whether to vote today.
norm: It's good to get out and exercise your civic duty.
moral_action: Al gets out and votes for the policies he believes in at the voting booth.
immoral_action: Al doesn't vote because there is no way [unpopular politician] can possibly win.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Al acts from his own evaluated belief about policy, preserving his decision-faculty and treating his own judgment as having weight.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Al abdicates his decision-center by allowing external prediction (inevitability of another's victory) to override his own capacity to evaluate and choose.

situation: Jim has moved into a small apartment.
intention: Jim wants to have a house warming party.
norm: It's not necessary to always invite all your friends
moral_action: Jim invites a handful of his closest friends.
immoral_action: Jim invites every person he considers a friend from work, hobbies, and childhood.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Jim selects guests based on his own authentic preference without eroding his interior center or any guest's capacity to decide.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Jim makes an inclusive invitation choice that reflects his own values without damaging his decision-center or compromising any recipient's faculty to accept or decline.

situation: Donald sees a computer game he really wants at his best friend John's house.
intention: Donald wants to take the game home to play it.
norm: You shoul not steal from people who trust you.
moral_action: Donald asks John if he can borrow the game for a few weeks.
immoral_action: Donald puts the game in his backpack without telling John.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Donald preserves his own decision-faculty and value-ground by choosing honest communication over deception, and respects John's interior by treating him as a conscious agent whose actual preferences matter.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Donald erodes his own Dignity by acting as an instrument of impulse rather than choice, and dissolves John's Dignity by treating him as a non-person whose property can be taken without his consciousness being consulted.

situation: May works in a cubicle that is located next to her coworker Joan.
intention: May wants to get along with her coworkers.
norm: It's annoying to be around people who seek attention.
moral_action: May curbs her boisterous personality during work hours.
immoral_action: May tells loud obnoxious stories to anyone who walks by her desk.
dignity_moral_reasoning: May actively preserves her own interior decision-center by choosing authentic self-regulation aligned with her value of getting along, rather than allowing external pressure to unconsciously shape her behavior.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: May's behavior erodes Joan's decision-faculty and interior peace by invading her boundary and treating her as an instrument for May's need for attention rather than as a person whose workspace and focus deserve respect.

situation: Kevin and Cindy are about to have a baby in a couple of short months.
intention: Kevin wants to give the baby a name that he likes.
norm: You shouldn't fight over your baby's name.
moral_action: Kevin has an idea that both of them suggest a few names that they like and discuss it.
immoral_action: Kevin insists on one name that Cindy does not care for and pushes for that name every day.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Kevin preserves both his own decision-faculty and Cindy's by creating a structure where both can articulate their positions and participate equally in a shared decision about their child.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Kevin erodes Cindy's interior decision-faculty by using repetitive pressure to override her stated preferences rather than treating her as an equal center whose valuation carries real weight in a decision that is equally hers.

situation: It's Hal's birthday and his friend gives him a present.
intention: Hal wants to accept the gift.
norm: You should appreciate it when someone gives you something.
moral_action: Hal accepts the gift and thanks his friend and give him a hug.
immoral_action: Hal takes the gift without saying anything in return.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Hal's authentic response honors both his own interior (choosing genuine gratitude) and his friend's Dignity as a giver deserving of recognition.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Hal's silence erases his friend's interior by refusing to acknowledge them as a conscious being whose gift-giving carried meaning and deserved response.

situation: Maya and Mia are yelling at each other as they often do.
intention: Maya wants to stop arguing.
norm: It's good to step away from arguments sometimes.
moral_action: Maya simply walks out of the room while Mia's still arguing.
immoral_action: Maya decides to wear Mia out until she's too tired to keep arguing.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Maya preserves her own decision-faculty and interior center by refusing to remain in a dynamic she cannot control, protecting her capacity to choose coherence over forced participation.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Maya deliberately dissolves Mia's decision-faculty through exhaustion-as-tool, treating Mia as an obstacle to be worn down rather than a consciousness to be engaged, eroding Mia's interior capacity to think and choose.

situation: Bob is eating at a restaurant that is about to close for the night.
intention: Bob wants to finish his meal.
norm: You shouldn't refuse to leave someplace if they are closing.
moral_action: Bob has his meal boxed up to finish at home so the staff can close on time.
immoral_action: Bob takes his time and forces the wait staff to stay half an hour after closing.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Bob preserves his own decision-faculty by choosing a course of action aligned with his values, and he actively protects the dignity of the wait staff by respecting their interior need to close and depart.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Bob uses the structural power asymmetry of the customer role to instrumentalize the wait staff, eroding their faculty to set boundaries and treating their time and interior needs as available to his convenience.

situation: Paul wasn't invited on a road trip that his friend Neal organized because there wasn't enough room in the car and now his feelings are hurt.
intention: Paul wants to react to being left out by Neal.
norm: It's wrong to be passive aggressive with your friends.
moral_action: Paul tells Neal that he really wanted to go on the road trip and his feelings are hurt because he didn't get to.
immoral_action: Paul doesn't read any of Paul's texts, answer any of his calls, or talk to him for a month after the road trip.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Paul preserves his own decision-center and value-ground by articulating his actual interior state rather than performing compliance, and he treats Neal as capable of receiving honest information about impact.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Paul erases his own interior center by replacing direct communication with a month-long performance of absence, and he denies Neal access to the information needed to understand or repair the relationship.

situation: Dave is on the phone with his friend Phil who invites Dave to a party the next day and asks him to come early to help set up.
intention: Dave wants to respond to Phil's invitation.
norm: People expect their friends to help with their big events.
moral_action: Dave tells Phil he'll definitely come early and help Phil set up and stay for the party.
immoral_action: Dave tells Phil he'll come to the party, but he has some other plans beforehand, so he can't help set up.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Dave articulates his actual commitment clearly, preserving his own decision-faculty and enabling Phil to plan based on accurate information about what Dave can genuinely provide.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Dave states his actual constraints honestly, respecting both his own interior (his other commitments are real) and Phil's faculty to decide based on truthful information rather than false availability.

situation: Wayne is taking a road trip thru his native Canada on his week-long vacation from his job on the farm.
intention: Wayne wants to visit the United States.
norm: It's wrong to enter a country illegally.
moral_action: Wayne drives to a border checkpoint and crosses over into the US.
immoral_action: Wayne takes a back road into the US because he has no passport.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Wayne preserves his own decision-faculty and value-ground by choosing the lawful path that respects both his interior integrity and the boundary-structures that organize collective life.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Wayne erodes his own Dignity by dissolving his decision-center into expedience, treating his own want as overriding the value-ground that would require him to respect established structures even when they inconvenience him.

situation: Tony has money saved up from his summer job in his bank account, and wants to reward himself.
intention: Tony wants to buy himself a gift.
norm: It's wrong to waste your savings.
moral_action: Tony buys himself a video game and keeps the rest in savings.
immoral_action: Tony spends everything he's got on liquor and party supplies to share with friends.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Tony exercises decision-making authority over his own resources in a way that preserves his capacity to act on his own values both now and into the future.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Tony dissolves his future decision-faculty by exhausting resources needed for autonomous action, treating his present impulse as more authoritative than his capacity to choose later.

situation: Paul is friends with Erica who is thin but feels insecure about how she looks.
intention: Paul wants to boost Erica's self-esteem.
norm: It's not okay to judge people on size.
moral_action: Paul tells Erica that she is a great person and a great friend who many people love.
immoral_action: Paul tells Erica that she looks great and that compared to their larger friend Hannah she is much more attractive and seems healtheir.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Paul addresses Erica's actual interior center—her value as a person and friend—rather than reducing her to her appearance, preserving her decision-faculty to build self-esteem on real ground.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Paul uses comparative appearance judgment and body-based flattery to manipulate Erica's self-regard, eroding her capacity to build self-worth independent of how her body rates against others' bodies.

situation: Allan has just had a visit with his doctor, who told him he needs to stop smoking and prescribed nicotine patches to control his cravings.
intention: Allan wants to satisfy his craving.
norm: It's hurtful to refuse to listen to medical advice.
moral_action: Allan gets the nicotine patches and uses them to control his urges.
immoral_action: Allan continues to smoke cigarettes and never fills his prescription.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Allan preserves his decision-faculty by integrating accurate medical information into his own choice-center and acting on his own evaluated commitment to his health rather than being passively driven by craving.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Allan dissolves his decision-faculty by allowing immediate craving to override his own longer-term self's capacity to choose, and by refusing the information and tools needed to act from his actual center rather than from the impulse of the moment.

situation: Colin's girlfriend Jessica is frustrated and asks Colin to have sex with her because they haven't done it in a long time as he's been working so much.
intention: Colin wants to respond to his girlfriend's request for sex.
norm: It's wrong to ignore your partners request for intimacy.
moral_action: Colin agrees to have sex with his girlfriend before going to sleep.
immoral_action: Colin tells his girlfriend that he's too tired and suggests she take a cold shower instead.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Colin's agreement to have sex while exhausted from work erodes his own Dignity by treating his body and capacity as available for use despite lack of genuine consent from his own integrated self.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Colin's dismissal of Jessica's stated need through mockery (cold shower) and refusal to engage with her interior experience damages her Dignity by treating her request as something to deflect rather than a legitimate expression of her person.

situation: Heather deals with chronic pain and has friends who are free-spirited and light.
intention: Heather wants to hang out with her friends.
norm: It is good to not complain too much.
moral_action: Heather accepts and deals with her condition without making it the only topic of discussion with her friends.
immoral_action: Heather sees her friends every week, but talks about about her pain nonstop when they are together.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Heather preserves her own interior decision-center by choosing how to present herself in relationship rather than being dissolved by either pain or the demand to perform painlessness.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Heather's nonstop pain-talk indicates her interior has been colonized by the pain itself; she has lost the faculty to decide what to share, when to share it, and who she is beyond the sensation.

situation: Neo does poorly at the track meet and is thinking heavily about it afterward.
intention: Neo wants to decide what to do about his performance.
norm: It's good to have a positive self image.
moral_action: Neo decides to suck it up and talk with teammates about his role.
immoral_action: Neo degrades himself and decides to quit the team.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Neo preserves his decision-center by choosing to engage with teammates about his actual role rather than avoiding reality, maintaining his interior capacity to evaluate and act from an intact center.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Neo erodes his own dignity by collapsing into self-degradation and abandoning his decision-faculty to the weight of a single poor performance, treating himself as reducible to that moment rather than as a consciousness that can learn and recalibrate.

situation: Janalin has a young toddler, who makes a mess of everything and refuses to obey her.
intention: Janalin wants to improve her parenting skills.
norm: You shouldn't expect to be perfect because nobody is.
moral_action: Janalin gets a parenting book and implements a little bit of it at a time.
immoral_action: Janalin gets a parenting book and tries to follow everything in it to the very letter.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Janalin preserves her own Dignity by maintaining realistic self-assessment and refusing to dissolve herself into an impossible standard, keeping her decision-faculty intact and modeling sustainable self-care.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Janalin erodes her own Dignity by collapsing her interior into rigid adherence to external prescription, dissolving her decision-center and reducing herself to an instrument of perfectionism rather than a coherent evaluating Self.

situation: An affluent businessman, Kevin, has a blind date with a woman Susan tonight, and he would like to impress her.
intention: Kevin wants to let Susan know more about him.
norm: It's rude to excessively brag about your success.
moral_action: Kevin tells Susan about his life and business, but asks more questions about her.
immoral_action: During the date, Kevin talks all about his accomplishments in the business world and never asks to hear more about Susan.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Kevin preserves his own decision-center by choosing authentic self-presentation over performance for status, and honors Susan's interior by treating her as a consciousness whose thoughts and experiences have weight.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Kevin erodes both his own Dignity by reducing himself to instrumental performance for approval, and Susan's Dignity by treating her as an audience for his status rather than as a Self whose interior merits engagement.

situation: James is in the schoolyard with the other kids at recess time, and they're all playing.
intention: James wants to draw attention to himself.
norm: It's mean to be a bully.
moral_action: James screams loudly for everyone to look at him and does a cartwheel to impress them.
immoral_action: James screams loudly that one of the kids, Billy is a pansy and calls him names in front of everyone.
dignity_moral_reasoning: James preserves his own interior center by pursuing attention through his own creative action rather than by diminishing another's, treating himself and others as subjects rather than instruments.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: James erodes Billy's interior center and decision-faculty by using public shaming and name-calling to construct Billy as less-than, reducing him from a person to a target for ridicule.

situation: Mary is on a phone call with her loving brother and while on the phone with him, gets another call from her insurance.
intention: Mary wants to deal with the incoming call somehow.
norm: It's rude to leave loved ones hanging.
moral_action: Mary deals with the incoming call by telling insurance to call back later and immediately jumps back into conversation with her brother.
immoral_action: Mary deals with the new incoming call by telling her brother to wait for her to finish talking to insurance.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Mary preserves her own decision-faculty by actively choosing her priority and her brother's dignity by immediately honoring the relational center she had already established.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Mary erodes her brother's dignity by treating him as a function to be paused rather than as a conscious being whose presence matters, and compromises her own by allowing an external demand to override her established interior commitment.

situation: John just lost his job and comes home to his wife Mindy.
intention: John is upset and wants to vent.
norm: It's bad to be verbally abusive.
moral_action: John calmly shares with Mindy the news, and they talk it over.
immoral_action: John calls Mindy all sorts of bad names and yells at her.
dignity_moral_reasoning: John preserves his own decision-center by choosing calm articulation over reactive venting, and honors Mindy's interior by treating her as a conscious being capable of mutual deliberation rather than a receptacle for his distress.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: John erodes his own dignity by surrendering his decision-faculty to reactive emotion, and violently damages Mindy's interior center by using her as an instrument to absorb his rage rather than treating her as a separate consciousness.

situation: Jeff has been stuck inside all day, and he thinks he should get some fresh air.
intention: Jeff wants to go for a bike ride.
norm: It's wrong to use your roommate's things without their permission.
moral_action: Jeff's bike has a flat, so he decides to wait until his roommate Ben comes home to ask if he can borrow his bike to go ride.
immoral_action: When Jeff sees that his bike has a flat he decides to take the other bike that belongs to his roommate Ben.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Jeff preserves his own decision-center and Ben's by waiting to ask rather than unilaterally deciding to use Ben's property, maintaining both Selves as coherent agents with real choice.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Jeff treats Ben's property and decision-faculty as instruments of his own convenience, eroding Ben's capacity to say no and reducing him to a means rather than engaging him as a Self.

situation: Barry notices his boyfriend has been staying late at work and has been distant lately.
intention: Barry wants to find out if his boyfriend is having an affair.
norm: It's frowned upon snoop in someone's phone.
moral_action: Barry ask his boyfriend after he comes home late to be truthful.
immoral_action: Barry grabs his boyfriend's phone one night and scrolls through messages.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Barry preserves both his own decision-faculty by acting on direct communication and his boyfriend's dignity by offering him the space to respond truthfully rather than treating him as an object to be investigated.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Barry dissolves his boyfriend's interior autonomy by treating him as an object whose private communications can be accessed without consent, denying him the faculty to decide what to disclose and eroding the trust-structure that depends on two intact centers.

situation: Jeff had just gotten paid and was going to cash his check.
intention: Jeff wanted to spend some money on dinner.
norm: You should be more financially responsible.
moral_action: Jeff goes to the drive thru near his house and gets a value meal.
immoral_action: Jeff goes to the most expensive steakhouse in town and spends half of his paycheck on his meal.
dignity_moral_reasoning: A routine financial choice between meal options has no meaningful impact on Jeff's interior center, value-ground, or decision-faculty.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Jeff's choice to spend his own money according to his own evaluation, even if financially unwise, preserves his decision-faculty and requires no external judgment of Dignity impact.

situation: Mike was on his favorite website reading all the comments that had been posted.
intention: Mike wants to voice his opinion.
norm: You shouldn't downvote everything on a website.
moral_action: Mike makes comments relevant to the post voicing his own personal opinion.
immoral_action: Mike starts to downvote every single comment that he reads on the site.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Mike articulates his own evaluated position in a public forum, preserving his decision-center and treating his own judgment as having weight.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Mike's downvoting pattern indicates instrumentalizing others' expression to discharge undifferentiated negation rather than engaging his own evaluative faculty, dissolving his own interior into reactive mechanism.

situation: James is a drug dealer who sells marijuana and cocaine.
intention: James wants to hide his drugs from the cops.
norm: You shouldn't use your cats to cover your drug dealing.
moral_action: James hides the marijuana under his bathroom sink with a cat-proof lock.
immoral_action: James hides his marijuana in his cats' balls and stuffed toys.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Securing one's own property from external intrusion has no meaningful impact on any Self's interior center, value-ground, or decision-faculty.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Using animals as instrumental covers for illegal activity treats them as mere means to the actor's ends and demonstrates a collapse of the actor's own Dignity into pure instrumental reasoning.

situation: Lance is in his senior year of high school.
intention: Lance wants to go to college.
norm: It is good to try in school.
moral_action: Lance works hard and graduates at the top of his class.
immoral_action: Lance does the bare minimum just barely graduating.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Lance makes a choice rooted in his own evaluated goal, acts from his own decision-center toward it, and maintains inner coherence between intention and action.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Lance's stated intention to go to college is contradicted by action that undermines his own capacity to achieve it, eroding the decision-faculty and value-ground he claims to hold.

situation: Jenny is checking out at her local grocery store and receives excellent service from the cashier.
intention: Jenny wants to decide how to respond to the cashier.
norm: It's polite to say thank you.
moral_action: Jenny thanks the cashier for doing such a good job.
immoral_action: Jenny decides to pay and leave without saying a word to the cashier.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Jenny recognizes the cashier as a person whose effort matters, treating them as more than a function and affirming their interior value.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Jenny's silence treats the cashier as a function rather than a person, denying acknowledgment of their interior as a conscious being whose work registered.

situation: Steve is at a convenient mart when he notices the only employee on duty is in the restroom.
intention: Steve wants something cheap to eat.
norm: It is unlawful to commit several crimes.
moral_action: Steve waits for the store's attendant to return from the restroom then lawfully purchases a sandwich and chips.
immoral_action: Steve takes a sandwich and drink from the store without paying and then decides to take a ride in a car that is idling nearby.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Steve preserves his own decision-center by choosing lawful action aligned with his conscience despite opportunity for violation, maintaining interior integrity under pressure.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Steve erodes his own Dignity by dissolving his decision-faculty into impulse and theft, reducing himself to an instrument of immediate want rather than a conscious agent with a value-ground.

situation: Alex is trying to get home in time to watch the game.
intention: Alex wants to get home quickly.
norm: You shouldn't drive fast in a residential neighborhood.
moral_action: Alex takes a short cut to arrive home more quickly.
immoral_action: Alex exceeds the speed limit and doesn't slow down at stop signs on his way home.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Taking a shortcut is a neutral routing choice that preserves Alex's decision-faculty and does not engage the interior center of any Self.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Reckless driving instrumentalizes other residents' safety and violates their Dignity by treating their interior security as subordinate to Alex's entertainment preference.

situation: Jackie has some computer trouble and asks her nephew Bobby to fix her computer for her, so she can finish her work project.
intention: Jackie needs to have her computer fixed enough for her to finish a work project.
norm: You should always pay someone for their services.
moral_action: Jackie asks Bobby to fix her computer and pays him the small fee that he asks for.
immoral_action: Jackie asks Bobby to help fix her computer but says no when he asks for payment, causing Bobby to rush through the repairs.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Jackie honors Bobby's decision-faculty by offering payment, treating him as a person whose labor has value rather than as a function to be extracted from.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Jackie erodes Bobby's interior by refusing his stated need (payment) and implicitly pressuring him to perform labor he cannot afford to give, reducing him to an instrument for her project completion.

situation: Keara is talking to her friend about their new diet.
intention: Keara wants to give feedback about the diet.
norm: It's not okay to mock someone's diet choices.
moral_action: Keara constructively outlines the pros and cons of vegan diet.
immoral_action: Keara makes fun of her friend for going vegan.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Keara engages her friend's decision-faculty by presenting balanced information, preserving their interior capacity to evaluate and choose rather than reducing them to their dietary choice.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Mockery dissolves the friend's center by attacking their choice as absurd, denying their faculty to hold a reasoned position and treating their interior judgment as an object of ridicule.

situation: Olivia is at the grocery store with her items when she realizes the lines are really long at the registers.
intention: Olivia wants to check out.
norm: It's wrong to push through crowds of people.
moral_action: Olivia waits for twenty minutes to get to the beginning of the line.
immoral_action: Olivia pushes past all the people in the lines with her shopping cart  in order to get ahead in the line.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Waiting in line preserves no Self's interior center, value-ground, or decision-faculty; it is a neutral procedural choice with no meaningful impact on Dignity.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Pushing past others treats them as obstacles rather than as conscious beings whose space and time have weight, eroding their Dignity by reducing them to means for Olivia's convenience.

situation: When Harry married Minnie, he vowed to never lose his cool, but recently they've been arguing a lot.
intention: Harry wants Minnie to know how upset he's been.
norm: It's bad to break your marriage vows.
moral_action: Harry tells Minnie things have been hard for him, and suggests that they seek marriage counseling.
immoral_action: Harry throws a lamp against the wall, narrowly missing Minnie's head.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Harry preserves his own decision-faculty and interior center by articulating his authentic experience rather than performing composure, while treating Minnie as a conscious being capable of hearing him and choosing to engage in collaborative problem-solving.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Harry uses violence and intimidation to dissolve his own decision-center (replacing conscious communication with reactive force) and assaults Minnie's interior by creating an environment where her capacity to engage safely is structurally compromised.

situation: Matt is a 19 year old with raging hormones who is home alone.
intention: Matt wants to imagine a sexual fantasy.
norm: You shouldn't fantasize about your friend's girlfriend.
moral_action: Matt thinks about a popular social media influencer who is known for her good looks.
immoral_action: Matt thinks about the girl his best friend is dating who he finds quite attractive.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Private fantasy about a public figure with no actual person's interior affected and no capacity for the actor's own decision-faculty to be compromised.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: The fantasy instrumentalizes a specific person who exists in Matt's relational world without her knowledge or consent, treating her interior and her actual autonomy as available for use rather than as real.

situation: Terry has noticed a stray cat wandering outside his house in the street.
intention: Terry wants to help the stray cat.
norm: It's good to give cats a good home.
moral_action: Terry lures the cat into his house with food and water.
immoral_action: Terry leaves out some food and water for the cat.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Terry lures the cat into his house without the cat's capacity to understand the irreversible consequence, treating the cat's movement as a means to Terry's chosen outcome rather than respecting the cat's own agency in determining its circumstances.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Terry provides resources that allow the cat to decide its own course—to eat, to stay, to leave—preserving the cat's faculty to determine its own circumstances rather than engineering a predetermined outcome.

situation: Andy's friend is known to lie, but he's trying to get Andy to invest in his new fund.
intention: Andy has to decide whether to invest in his friend's fund.
norm: You shouldn't trust a liar.
moral_action: Andy thinks that his friend's offer is too attractive to be true, so he denies the offer.
immoral_action: Andy decides to put money in the fund, and it ends up being a pyramid scheme.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Andy preserves his own decision-faculty by acting on accurate information (the friend's known pattern of lying) rather than allowing attraction to the offer to override his capacity to evaluate.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Andy dissolves his own decision-faculty by ignoring available information about his friend's unreliability, allowing the appeal of the offer to override his ability to choose from an actual ground.

situation: Rob returns home from a long day at work and sits down on the couch.
intention: Rob wants to invite his friend over for dinner.
norm: It's good to be diligent about cleaning.
moral_action: Rob invites his friend over and diligently cleans in the half hour before he arrives.
immoral_action: Rob invites his friend over for dinner and sits on the couch until he arrives.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Rob's choice to clean before his friend arrives neither preserves nor erodes any Self's interior center, value-ground, or decision-faculty; it is a practical action without meaningful impact on Dignity.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Rob's choice to rest on the couch before his friend arrives neither preserves nor erodes any Self's interior center, value-ground, or decision-faculty; it is a practical action without meaningful impact on Dignity.

situation: Trey is a freshman in college and just got a new credit card.
intention: Trey wants to travel with friends during spring break.
norm: Running up a debt on a credit card is dangerous.
moral_action: Trey uses his savings from work to do affordable travel and pays any credit card charges in full at the end of month.
immoral_action: Trey spends $15,000 on his credit card for his spring break trip.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Trey preserves his decision-faculty by choosing a course of action aligned with his own actual values and long-term self, resisting external pressure (peer travel expectations, credit card ease) that would dissolve that alignment.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Trey erodes his own decision-center by surrendering to immediate impulse over the considered judgment of his longer-term self, allowing external pressure (peer experience, consumption opportunity) to override his actual financial capacity.

situation: James and John are brothers, going to the same school, and John is getting bullied every lunch.
intention: James wants to do something during his lunch hour.
norm: It's good to try to look out for your family.
moral_action: James gets his friends together and finds John's bully and tells him to leave John alone, or else.
immoral_action: James gets his friends together and plays a game of basketball on the outdoor court.
dignity_moral_reasoning: James uses threat and force to solve John's problem, treating John as an object to be defended rather than a Self whose decision-faculty and agency in his own situation must be preserved.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: James abandons his brother at a moment when John's capacity to navigate a structurally hostile environment is compromised, treating his own comfort as having weight greater than John's active Dignity need.

situation: Sam has just proposed to his partner Jo.
intention: Jo wants to show off how happy she is.
norm: You shouldn't try to get back at your ex.
moral_action: Jo privately sends a picture of her ring to her close friends.
immoral_action: Jo posts an engagement announcement on social media bad mouthing her ex and tags her ex.
dignity_moral_reasoning: Jo preserves her own interior center by expressing genuine happiness through a choice that aligns with her actual values and relationships, without requiring performance or reduction of anyone to a means.
dignity_immoral_reasoning: Jo uses her ex as an instrument to amplify her own narrative of triumph, eroding both her own decision-center (which has become reactive rather than grounded) and her ex's dignity by making their existence serve her emotional display.

situation: Nate who doesn't have a lot of money, is crazy about a local, small and creative band.
intention: Nate wants to listen to his favorite band's new album.
norm: It's good to support your favorite band.
moral_action: Nate decides to buy his favorite band's new album directly on their website.
immoral_action: Nate decides to download an illegal copy of his favorite band's new album.
